### AIDA

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/aida/
Date: 2026-08-12. Read: 11 min.

AIDA claims that a buyer passes through attention, interest, desire and action in that order, and that a message should push them along it. The attribution to E. St. Elmo Lewis in 1898 rests on one uncited sentence in a 1925 textbook; the four steps first appear in salesmanship magazines of 1903 and 1904 under other names [1][3]. AIDA itself has never been tested. Its descendants have: a review of 250 studies found little support for any fixed sequence [7], and a seven-year test of 178 brands found the think-first order fitted 7 per cent of brands where any single order fitted [11]. Use AIDA as a checklist for one piece of copy. Stop using it as a map of how buyers move.

## Origin

The usual story is that Lewis, an American advertising man, set out three steps in 1898 and added a fourth later. It comes from Edward K. Strong's *The Psychology of Selling and Advertising* (McGraw-Hill, 1925), which says that in 1898 Lewis "used the slogan, 'Attract attention, maintain interest, create desire,'" in an advertising course in Philadelphia, took the idea from William James, and "later on" added "get action" [1, p. 9]. Strong repeats the claim on page 348. He gives no source either time.

Strong was solving a training problem. America had become a buyer's market and selling had to be taught: his count of salesmanship books runs from one in 1869 to 267 in the 1910s [1, p. 8]. AIDA was a mnemonic for salesmen and copywriters, never a finding about buyers.

The attribution has now been checked against Lewis's own writing. Akinori Iwamoto read every surviving Lewis article and book from 1897 to 1910, including the *Inland Printer* columns written as Musgrove, and found no text in which Lewis prints the slogan [3]. The nearest is 1899: an advertisement "will attract, interest and convince" [3, Table 1]. The only record of Lewis saying the four words is a 1910 report of a speech in which he describes hearing "a writer" say them [3, p. 13].

The sequence was in print by then, under other names. Frank Dukesmith's magazine *Salesmanship* set out "securing attention," "arousing the interest," "creating desire," and "closing the sale" in June 1903 [3, Table 2]. Arthur Sheldon's correspondence school taught attention, interest, desire and "resolve to buy" from 1903 and, by 1910, attention, interest, desire, action [3, Tables 2 and 5]. The first orderly printing of all four AIDA words Iwamoto could find is Seth Brown, December 1904 [3, p. 3]. Barry and Howard's 1990 review, the standard academic history, repeats Strong's version [5, p. 123, as quoted in 3], and Kotler's *Marketing Management* has carried the Strong citation since 1972 [3, p. 2].

Established: the acronym and the Lewis story entered the literature through Strong in 1925; the four steps were a salesmanship convention by 1904; Lewis wrote in threes. Not established: that Lewis originated anything in 1898.

## What the evidence shows

There is no empirical literature on AIDA as such. The tests exist for its descendant, the hierarchy of effects, so that is what can be reported.

Lavidge and Steiner (1961) turned the slogan into a measurement proposal. Their four-page *Journal of Marketing* article lists six steps, awareness, knowledge, liking, preference, conviction and purchase, groups them into cognitive, affective and conative functions, and argues for measuring advertising at each step rather than by sales alone [6][11, p. 8]. It is a theorist's claim, not a finding: the article reports no test of the sequence. Palda (1966) coined "hierarchy of effects" and was the first to evaluate it [11, p. 2].

The largest review is Vakratsas and Ambler (1999). They read more than 250 journal articles and books and concluded that "there is little support for any hierarchy, in the sense of temporal sequence, of effects" [7, abstract]. They proposed dropping the sequence and studying advertising in a space of affect, cognition and experience, with position set by context [7].

The most direct test came twenty years later. Pauwels, Valenti, Srinivasan, Yildirim and Vanhuele modelled weekly data for 178 fast-moving consumer goods brands in 18 categories over seven years, with survey measures of cognition, affect and experience alongside sales [11]. Three results matter. A sequence does exist: for 94 per cent of brands an ordered model beat the simultaneous one, which fitted none of the 178 [11, p. 21]. The order is not AIDA's: among the 90 brands where one sequence was statistically best, affect came first in 42 per cent, and the think-feel-do order AIDA assumes fitted 6 brands, 7 per cent [11, Table 6]. And the last factor in whatever sequence operates explains 56 per cent of the sales variation attributable to the three, the first only 16 per cent [11, p. 25].

Ehrenberg reached a similar shape by another route in 1974. His awareness, trial, reinforcement account holds that for established brands of frequently bought goods advertising's "main role is to reinforce feelings of satisfaction with brands already bought" [12]. The Ehrenberg-Bass Institute's position today, in Sharp's words: "The dominant way that advertising works is by refreshing, and occasionally building, memory structures that improve the chance of the brand being recalled and/or noticed in buying situations," and "most sales typically come from people who had not formed an intention" [13]. On this account there is no desire stage. There is memory, and there is the buying occasion.

Industry survey data describe the same buyer. In the 2024 Edelman-LinkedIn study of 3,500 B2B decision makers, 75 per cent said one piece of thought leadership had led them to research a product or service they were not previously considering, and 70 per cent of C-suite respondents said one had made them question whether to keep a current supplier [19]. The content did not find an interest stage. It made one.

Binet and Field's analysis of 996 IPA Effectiveness Awards cases separates the two mechanisms AIDA fuses [14, p. 10]. Rational messaging produces the bigger short-term sales effect and decays; emotional priming produces a smaller immediate effect that accumulates [15, slides 13 and 14]. Emotional campaigns reporting very large profit growth rise from 13 per cent at one year to 43 per cent at three years or more; rational campaigns from 10 to 23 per cent [14, Figure 52][15, slide 16]. "Feelings towards brands outlast memories of facts and figures about the brand" [14, p. 53].

Cialdini addresses the first letter. *Pre-Suasion* argues that the factor most likely to determine a choice "is the one that has been elevated in attention (and thereby in privilege) at the moment of decision" [16, chapter 2 summary]. To get action "it's not necessary to alter a person's beliefs or attitudes or experiences," only "what's prominent in that person's mind at the moment of decision" [16, chapter 1]. The principles of *Influence* are likewise levers, not stages [17]. Attention, for Cialdini, is not the entrance to a corridor. It is the decision.

## The challenge

The empirical challenge is real but aimed at the family, not the member. Nobody has published a test of AIDA because there is nothing in it to test: four states and an asserted order, with no measures and no timing.

The strongest published critique is Weilbacher's 2001 *Journal of Advertising Research* essay: hierarchy models do not describe what advertising does to people, do not describe how it works in markets, and while advertising is thought about in hierarchy terms its true effects will not be measured [8]. Barry replied in defence of the hierarchy as a guide for practice and research [9]. Weilbacher's rejoinder: "If a widely accepted theory has not been proven over the course of 100 years, isn't it time to say so?" [10, p. 49, as quoted in 11, p. 3].

The positions are worth stating exactly. Vakratsas and Ambler: no temporal hierarchy is supported [7]. Pauwels and colleagues: a hierarchy is supported, it varies by brand and category, affect usually leads, and the fully simultaneous model fits no brand [11]. Ehrenberg and Sharp: the intermediate states are mostly beside the point, because advertising works on memory and most buying happens without prior intention [12][13]. Binet and Field: emotional and rational effects run on different clocks, so any single sequence is a category error [14]. Barry: the hierarchy remains useful as a planning device [9].

Two things are not in dispute. No body of evidence supports a fixed attention-interest-desire-action order across brands. And every camp agrees that purchase feeds back into the first step, which a one-way sequence cannot represent [11, p. 2][12].

## Where practitioners get it wrong

**Reading it as a journey.** AIDA describes what one message should do. The funnel reads it as what one buyer does, over weeks, across channels, one stage at a time. The funnel is a practitioner convention with no author and no test. Stage-gated content, where a prospect is "moved" from awareness assets to consideration assets before seeing an offer, is built on it. Pauwels' data say the first factor explains 16 per cent of sales variation and the last 56 per cent [11, p. 25]; Sharp's say most buyers never formed an intention [13]. Gartner's survey of 750 B2B buyers found that buying groups spend 17 per cent of a purchase meeting any potential supplier and 45 per cent researching on their own, that a complex purchase involves six to ten decision makers, and that the six buying jobs are revisited in loops rather than completed in order [18].

The channel side of the picture is the same. McKinsey's B2B Pulse counted the distinct channels a buyer uses across one purchase at five in 2016, 7.5 in 2019 and ten in December 2021, and in its April 2024 wave of 3,942 decision makers found between 30 and 37 per cent of time in each of in-person, remote and digital self-service at every one of four buying stages, whichever buyer type was asked [20]. No stage owns a channel, so a content plan that assigns channels to stages is assigning them to a fiction.

**Reading it as a measurement plan.** Dashboards that report awareness, consideration, intent and purchase as a cascade assume the order they are meant to test. Attitude measures are unstable: the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute reports about a 50 per cent chance that a person states the same attitude to a brand in two surveys [13]. The leaks in such a cascade are partly measurement noise.

**Reading attention as a hook for an argument.** The AIDA copy formula treats attention as the door and the rational case as the room. Binet and Field's rational campaigns win at six months and lose at three years [14, p. 53]. Cialdini's work says what is in mind at the moment of decision does the deciding [16]. The error is spending the creative budget on the argument and the media budget on the hook. HubSpot's survey of 1,400 sales professionals reports that 96 per cent of prospects have researched before their first conversation with a rep, and 88 per cent already know the company [22]; the hook has been and gone before the seller arrives.

**Our own observation.** In the smallest of the supply chain group's four markets, prospects doubted the group had a genuine local presence, and sales spent the first ten minutes of every call proving it did. We filmed their own people at their own site in the local language, no studio, no script. Engagement ran more than three times that of produced static work, and it cost less to make. The commercial effect sat elsewhere: prospects arrived already past the first step. The sequence did not run attention, interest, desire. Proof removed a question, and the conversation started further in.

## What to do with it

1. Write AIDA into the brief as a copy checklist for a single asset, nowhere else. Check: the brief's journey section cites something other than AIDA. 2. Remove any gate that withholds an offer until a prospect has consumed earlier-stage content. Check: every prospect can reach the offer from any first touch. 3. Measure cognition, affect and experience in the same quarterly survey wave and record which moves first for your brand. Check: all three sit in one instrument. 4. Set reach targets on the category, not the CRM. Check: the media plan states a share of category buyers reached, including non-customers. 5. Run two evaluation clocks: activation copy at three to six months, brand priming at three years. Check: each campaign line carries its window. 6. Before writing any message, write one line on what the audience will be attending to at the moment of exposure. Check: the line is in the creative brief. 7. Stop citing Lewis 1898. Cite Strong 1925 for the acronym and Dukesmith, Sheldon and Brown 1903 to 1904 for the sequence. Check: the deck footnote.

### Brand equity

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/brand-equity/
Date: 2026-08-06. Read: 11 min.

Brand equity is the claim that a name adds value beyond what the product does, and that this value can be built, measured and banked. Aaker (1991) listed the assets; Keller (1993) located them in the customer's memory. The evidence supports the core claim: perceived quality and some brand attribute scores carry information about future returns, and three of four survey pillars track sales-based equity. The weak points are measurement and loyalty. Practitioners should track equity as behaviour first, survey second, and never as a league-table valuation.

## Origin

The term arrived through the finance department. Keller (1993) opens with two motivations for studying brand equity: a financial one, "to estimate the value of a brand more precisely for accounting purposes" or for mergers and acquisitions, and a strategic one, to improve marketing productivity [2, p. 1]. Acquirers in the 1980s were paying multiples of book value for consumer companies, and nobody could say what the premium bought.

The academic conversation was formalised at a Marketing Science Institute conference in Austin, Texas, on 1 to 3 March 1988, summarised as MSI Report 88-104, "Defining, Measuring and Managing Brand Equity" [4]. Farquhar (1989) supplied the working definition: brand equity is "the 'added value' with which a brand endows a product", viewable from the firm, the trade or the consumer [3].

Aaker's Managing Brand Equity (1991) sorted that added value into five asset categories: brand loyalty, name awareness, perceived quality, brand associations, and other proprietary assets such as patents and channel relationships [1]. Keller (1993) moved the unit of analysis into the customer's head. His definition, quoted once here, is "the differential effect of brand knowledge on consumer response to the marketing of the brand" [2, p. 2]. A brand has positive equity when consumers react more favourably to a marketing action for the named brand than to the same action for an unnamed version [2, p. 2]. Brand knowledge is awareness plus image, and image is a set of "favorable, strong, and unique brand associations" [2, p. 1].

Kotler's Marketing Management carried the Keller model into the standard curriculum from the 12th edition (2006), with Keller as co-author [8].

## What the evidence shows

**Perceived quality predicts stock returns.** Aaker and Jacobson (1994) asked whether a survey measure of perceived quality (Total Research's EquiTrend database) explained movements in firm value beyond what return on investment already explained. Controlling for economy-wide factors and ROI, they found "a positive relationship between stock return and changes in quality perceptions" [11, abstract]: the survey carried information the accounts did not.

**Some survey pillars carry financial information, others do not.** Mizik and Jacobson (2008) repeated the exercise with the five pillars of Young and Rubicam's Brand Asset Valuator. Relevance and energy added information to accounting measures in explaining stock return; esteem and knowledge did not, because their effect was already in current-term accounting results [12, abstract].

**Consumer-based and sales-based equity partly align.** Datta, Ailawadi and van Heerde (2017) built the most direct test to date: ten years of IRI scanner data and BAV survey data for 290 brands in 25 packaged-goods categories. Sales-based brand equity (SBBE) is the brand intercept in a market-share model. The abstract reports "a fairly strong positive association of SBBE with three dimensions of CBBE, relevance, esteem, and knowledge, but a slight negative correspondence with the fourth dimension, energized differentiation" [13]. A published summary gives the correlations as 0.35, 0.39, 0.53 and -0.14 respectively [14].

Brands high in knowledge, esteem and relevance gained more from price cuts and distribution gains; differentiated brands showed a larger advertising response; and knowledge did not buy a price premium [15]. Ailawadi: "Academics as well as managers often regard a brand's ability to charge a price premium as the single most important indicator of brand equity, but we find that it is not" [15].

**Brand building reduces price sensitivity, slowly.** Binet and Field's meta-analysis of the IPA Databank (996 campaigns, 700 brands, 83 categories) reports the share of campaigns with a very large reduction in price sensitivity by the number of very large brand effects the same campaign recorded: 1% with none, 3% with one, 5% with two, 8% with three, 11% with four or more [21, slide 7]. Pricing effects also rise with campaign duration up to three years [21, slide 5]. Binet in 2023: "There are no examples of short-term activation campaigns lowering the price sensitivity of a brand" [22].

Cialdini did not address brand equity as a construct, but three of his principles describe how Aaker's associations get made: social proof (chapter 4), authority (chapter 5) and commitment and consistency (chapter 7) of Influence, 2021 edition [23]. That is a claim about mechanism, not a finding about equity.

**Buyers say trust decides purchases at the level of quality and price.** Edelman's 2025 brand trust survey, 15,042 people in 15 markets, asked which attributes of a brand are important or a deal breaker when buying. "I trust it" scored 88%, level with best quality and value for money, both 88% [30, p. 14]. The 2026 wave repeated the tie at 88%, 89% and 88% [31, p. 12]. That is stated intention, the survey side of the ledger, not the behaviour side.

**Industry valuers report large brand premiums, as associations.** McKinsey's B2B branding analysis has strong brands outperforming weak ones by 20% [33]. Brand Finance puts the 300 most valuable B2B brands at $4 trillion, 11% of their owners' enterprise value, and reports a 65% premium in forward price-to-earnings ratios for the stronger-branded businesses [32]. Across its Global 500, brand value averages around 20% of enterprise value [26]. None of these separates the brand from the business that carries it, which is the problem the next section takes up.

## The challenge

The three challenges do not say brands add no value. They say the number on your dashboard may not be what you think it is.

**The word means three things.** Feldwick (1996) sorted the uses into (a) the total value of a brand as a separable asset when sold or put on a balance sheet, (b) the strength of consumers' attachment to a brand, and (c) the associations and beliefs the consumer holds about it [5, as summarised in 6]: brand valuation, brand strength, brand description. The commercial valuation systems mix all three. Interbrand starts from economic profit, multiplies by a Role of Brand Index, and discounts at a rate set by a 0 to 100 Brand Strength score across ten factors [9]. Kantar BrandZ starts from parent-company earnings, isolates a branded intangible portion, and multiplies by a Brand Contribution score from its Meaningful, Different, Salient survey [10]. Both are financial value times a survey multiplier. Brand Finance's Global 500 is a third such system: $10.4 trillion across 500 brands in 2026, up 11% in a year, with the top ten brands holding 27% of the total [26]. None of the three is Keller's differential effect. Interbrand's Best Global Brands also requires a Brand Strength Score of 50 or above for entry [9]. A league table with an entry gate is a marketing artefact, not a measurement. The tables are also volatile in a way beliefs are not: Kantar's Top 100 total fell 20% in 2023 and rose 29% and 22% in the two years after, a pattern Kantar itself attributes to the stock market [24].

**Attitudinal equity may be restating market share.** This is the Ehrenberg-Bass position. Double jeopardy, first documented by McPhee in 1963 and reviewed by Ehrenberg, Goodhardt and Barwise (1990), says a smaller brand has fewer buyers and those buyers buy it slightly less often [16]. The Institute's restatement: "Double Jeopardy tells us that loyalty is largely a predictable function of market share" [17]. Sharp draws the consequence for surveys: "Larger brands tend to score higher on any image question, because they will have more customers among the survey respondents" [18, quoted in 28]. On the Institute's site: "attitudes follow behaviour" and "the effect of behaviour on attitudes is much stronger" than the reverse [19]. His sharpest line targets the industry built on Aaker's first asset: "Brand equity consultancies make money flattering owners of large market share brands... that they are not just large but also strong with attitudinally committed consumers" [18, quoted in 27]. Sharp does not deny loyalty exists; he calls it "a natural part of buying behaviour" [19, citing [How Brands Grow](/readings/how-brands-grow-byron-sharp/) p. 92]. He denies it is an independent asset you can grow ahead of penetration. Kantar's Blueprint for Brand Growth, drawn from 6.5 billion BrandZ and Worldpanel data points, reports that brands that are meaningfully different to more people have five times the market penetration [29]. Read from the Ehrenberg-Bass side, that is the same correlation with the arrow reversed.

Sharp and Romaniuk replace the asset list with two properties. Mental availability "means that buyers easily think of the brand when buying and recognize it quickly"; physical availability "means that buyers can buy the brand in a variant, quantity and price that matches their purchasing needs" [20]. Against Aaker, this keeps awareness and associations, drops perceived quality as a driver, and demotes loyalty from cause to consequence.

**The tests are partial.** Datta and colleagues found alignment for three pillars, not four, and it was moderate. Mizik and Jacobson found two pillars informative, not five. Aaker and Jacobson found one measure informative among large corporate brands. Datta's team describe association, not cause [13]. Anyone who tells you a tracker score predicts revenue is ahead of the published evidence.

## Where practitioners get it wrong

**Reading a valuation ranking as a management score.** The Interbrand and Kantar numbers are financial value times a multiplier. A brand that grows revenue with unchanged perceptions climbs the table; one whose company reports lower profit falls, whatever its buyers think. Feldwick's first meaning is being sold as his second [5, 6]. Apple's brand was worth $470.9 billion to Interbrand in October 2025, $608 billion to Brand Finance in January 2026 and $1.38 trillion to Kantar in May 2026 [25, 26, 24]; Kantar ranks Google above Apple, the other two do not.

**Treating tracker "loyalty" and "favourability" as assets to grow.** Double jeopardy predicts most of the variation in these metrics from share alone [16, 17]. The useful diagnostic is the deviation from the double jeopardy line, not the raw score. Self-report is no better: The CMO Survey asks marketing leaders to rate the change in their own brand value, and the February 2025 wave averaged +8.4% across 167 answers, with no instrument behind the number [34, p. 43].

**Assuming equity buys a price premium on its own.** Datta's team found high knowledge did not support a premium in packaged goods [15]. Binet and Field found price effects arrive only with multiple large brand effects and only over years [21]. Raising price the quarter after a good tracker wave is a bet the evidence does not back.

**Our own observation.** Five projects, one developer behind them, and the developer brand was the least communicated asset in the group. Fifteen years, thousands of apartments delivered, energy efficiency as standard: none of it was being said. We gave the company its own campaign, separate from any project, because in a cautious market the most useful thing a developer can prove is that it will still be there at completion. We cannot yet show that equity in a price. Enquiries are not reservations, and the link to signed contracts sits in the developer's sales data, still to be joined.

## What to do with it

1. Write down which of Feldwick's three meanings you are measuring before you buy a tracker or a valuation [5]. If the answer is "all three", you have not decided. 2. Estimate sales-based equity from your own data: the brand intercept in a share or choice model after controlling for price, promotion, distribution and advertising [13]. Failing that, use revenue premium over a private-label equivalent. 3. Plot every attitudinal metric against penetration for your category and report the residual, not the level [16, 17]. 4. Track awareness and associations as Keller specified them, favourable, strong and unique, by category entry point [2, 20]. Drop indices that average across them. 5. Put a behavioural measure next to every survey measure on the same page: penetration, repeat rate, distribution, price paid [12]. 6. If the objective is pricing power, plan for three years or more and for brand-building that produces several measurable brand effects: that is the only pattern in the IPA data associated with large falls in price sensitivity [21, 22]. 7. Retire the phrase "grow loyalty" unless your loyalty metric sits below the double jeopardy line for your share [17]. Otherwise the plan is "grow penetration" under another name.

Figure: Campaigns with four or more very large brand effects were eleven times as likely to report a very large fall in price sensitivity. Pricing power in the IPA data is a downstream effect of accumulated brand effects, which is the strongest published support for treating equity as a long-term asset and the clearest warning against expecting it quickly.. ## 02 History of advertising

A timeline of the moments that changed how advertising and marketing reach people, from the first agency to the first AI answer. Who invented advertising, when the first commercials ran, and what each change did.

### 1841. Who invented the advertising agency

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/1841-who-invented-the-advertising-agency/
Date: 2026-09-07. Read: 10 min.

Volney Palmer opened the first US ad agency in 1841, paid by the newspapers. How that commission shaped agencies to the Mad Men era, and what replaced it.

## The moment

Philadelphia, 1841. Volney B. Palmer takes a room at the north-west corner of Third and Chestnut streets and puts himself in the city directory as the agent of newspapers across the country [2]. A merchant who wants his notice in the country papers walks in, picks the towns, hands over his own copy and his money. Palmer sends the copy and the money on to the publishers and keeps a quarter of what they are paid [4]. He writes nothing. He is paid by the papers, so he advises what the papers need. By 1849 he has a paper of his own and an offer to draw up advertisements for merchants with no time to write them [7]. The business has every part of a modern agency except a client who pays the agent.

## What came before

The problem was arithmetic. There were 75 newspapers in the United States in 1790, more than 360 in 1820 and more than 1,400 by 1840. A wholesaler who wanted the farm towns could not write to a thousand editors, and the editors could not sell their own space. Someone had to stand in the middle [6].

London had stood there first. William Tayler advertised himself in 1786 as agent of the country printers and booksellers. George Reynell opened an office in Chancery Lane in 1812 to place legal notices, and his firm stayed in the family for six generations. Both worked for the printers. Palmer ran the same business in America, and the record does not settle the year he started. The Smithsonian guide to the Ayer records and Duke's Hartman Center say 1841, Tungate and Hower say 1842, and Fox says 1843 [10, 11, 7, 8, 2, 6, 1].

The space brokers who followed him refined the model and kept its flaw. George P. Rowell sold ads for a theatre programme in the holiday season of 1864, cleared $600 in a few weeks, and opened his own agency in Boston the following year, buying space in bulk and reselling it by the inch. He then published the first directory of American newspapers with circulations and rates, more than 5,000 titles. William James Carlton began canvassing for several papers in December 1864, mainly Methodist magazines; James Walter Thompson joined him as bookkeeper in 1868 and bought the one-man firm in 1878 for $500. Daniel Lord and Ambrose Thomas formed Lord and Thomas in Chicago in 1881, still a space broker. All of them lived on the publisher's discount, which ran from 10 to 50 per cent depending on the paper and how quietly the deal was done [1, 2, 9, 14, 3, 5].

## What it changed

The turn came in Philadelphia too. Francis Wayland Ayer had spent a year soliciting advertisements on commission for a Baptist weekly when, in 1869, he persuaded his father Nathan to put $250 into N. W. Ayer and Son [7]. In 1875 he offered a Pennsylvania rose grower, Dingee and Conard, what he called the open contract. The advertiser gave Ayer a budget and the authority to buy whichever space served it best; Ayer bought at the published rate, took no secret discounts, and was paid a set commission that advertiser, agent and publisher all knew. Fox marks it as the end of buying space low and selling it high [5][1]. Two years later Ayer bought Coe, Wetherill and Company, Palmer's successor firm, and could claim the oldest line in the trade [7].

What a marketer could do the day after was hire someone who worked for him. Ayer proved it in 1880 by researching the grain output and farm papers of the whole country before pitching a Michigan maker of threshing machines, and refusing to sell the resulting book to anyone who was not a client [6]. The commission rate settled at 15 per cent of the gross rate by the early 1890s, and the American Association of Advertising Agencies, founded in 1917, fixed it there in 1918 [4]. Ayer almost always got the full 15 per cent; around 1898 Lord and Thomas got less, and Albert Lasker's answer was to write the copy himself [3]. In 1904 he hired John E. Kennedy, a Canadian-born copywriter who told him advertising was salesmanship in print, at $16,000 a year when Lasker's copywriters earned about $1,400 [3]. By 1906 Lasker could say that ninety per cent of the thought, energy and cost of running the agency went into copy [5].

Media buying, research and creative work, bundled and paid for out of one cut of the media money. That is the full-service agency.

The mechanism had a flaw its inventors knew. Paid on spend, an agency earns more when the client spends more, and nothing on advice to spend less or somewhere that pays no commission. Fees fixed that and introduced the next flaw, since an agency paid for hours earns more when the work takes longer. The ANA's 2022 survey found 82 per cent of marketers paying by fee, and among advertisers spending $500 million or more a year, 53 per cent paying fixed or output-based fees, up from 5 per cent in 2016 [20]. The number of agencies did not shrink while the money changed hands.

## The Mad Men thread

The series gives readers a mid-sized Madison Avenue shop in 1960 that bills its clients a percentage of what it spends on their behalf. The real agencies did, and the pressure on the model was already public. In February 1956 the Four A's signed a consent decree with the Justice Department's antitrust chief, Stanley Barnes, agreeing to end the requirement that members collect a 15 per cent commission, to drop its ban on rebating, and to stop policing the industry. In November 1960 Shell asked Ogilvy, Benson and Mather to work for a fee instead; the fee was the actual cost of running the account plus 25 per cent, and the New York Times reported it as a surprise. To its advocates, Fox writes, the fee put the agency on the footing of an attorney or physician, paid for work done rather than for what the agent could spend [12, 1, 4].

Palmer's office became Coe, Wetherill, which became part of Ayer in 1877. Carlton's firm became J. Walter Thompson, which led the industry in billings from 1922 to 1972. Lasker became a one-quarter partner in Lord and Thomas in 1904 and sole owner in 1912, and in December 1942 worked out a plan to dissolve it. Foote, Cone and Belding opened at the turn of the year with three equal partners and the same staff in Chicago, New York, Los Angeles and San Francisco. The agency in the series is invented. The commission it lives on was built in these offices [7, 14, 3, 13].

What the commission had been doing showed once it was gone. In the 1990s the holding companies spun their media departments out as separate buying companies, MindShare at WPP, OMD and PhD at Omnicom, Zenith at Saatchi and Cordiant. By 2010 only 3 per cent of ANA members still used commission in any agreement; by 2016 it was back to 12 per cent, almost all of it for media buying and programmatic work. The medium Palmer brokered was by then losing most of its advertising money [9, 19].

The four largest groups descended from this lineage, Publicis, WPP, Omnicom and Interpublic, reported 2024 revenue of $62.6 billion between them. The publisher's discount is gone. What replaced it is still a cut of what clients spend on attention [23, 24, 25, 26].

## Applied: if you are a B2C brand

Say you sell a mid-price skincare line and must decide between an agency, a freelancer network and an in-house team. Before you look at a single portfolio, ask each option who pays it and on what. An agency paid a percentage of media has Palmer's incentive, to grow the spend and steer it to where the percentage is earned. An agency on labour fees has the opposite one, and will staff your account generously. A freelancer network paid per deliverable has Ayer's 1880 incentive in miniature, to do the work up front and win the next brief, which suits you until the brief needs a plan nobody is paid to write. An in-house team on salary has no reason to prefer one channel to another, which is also why it rarely challenges the channel it already knows.

So write the contract before the pitch. We sit on the agency side of this table, and the compensation clause is the page nobody reads at a pitch, on either side. Ask for the media plan with the agency's own earnings shown line by line, as the ANA has pushed for since its 2016 transparency work. If the plan leans towards channels where the agency earns a commission, you are looking at the problem Ayer's open contract solved in 1875, and it gets fixed in the contract [19].

## Applied: if you are a B2B brand

Say you make industrial pumps and your media is trade press, LinkedIn and two conferences a year. Nobody earns a commission on any of it. Media-neutral advice, in this market, means advice from someone whose income does not change when you move money from the stand to the sponsored post. That is a different thing from advice that is right.

Ayer's 1875 contract put the neutrality in the terms, so put yours there too. Pay for the plan as a fixed deliverable with a stated scope, so the adviser is not rewarded for a longer plan. Pay for execution separately and keep the right to execute in-house, as 30 per cent of ANA members already do for programmatic buying. Then test the adviser as the threshing-machine maker could test Ayer in 1880. Ask for the research before the recommendation, and read whether it argues from your buyers or from what the adviser happens to sell [22].

## What to do with it

1. Before any agency, consultant or network pitches you, write down the base each one will be paid on: media spend, hours, deliverables or outcomes. Reject any proposal where that base is not written into the contract. 2. Require a media plan that shows the agency's own revenue on every line. Any channel where the agency earns more than its blended rate needs a written justification before you approve the plan. 3. If you pay for hours, cap the hours per deliverable in the scope and check the timesheets against the cap every quarter. That is the control the ANA's 2022 respondents were moving towards with fixed fees [20]. 4. Keep media buying and advice as separate clauses so you can move either without moving both. The 1990s unbundling served the agencies; make it serve you. 5. Once a year, have someone with no stake in the plan re-run the channel allocation from the buyer evidence alone, and compare it with the plan you bought.

Figure: Commission survives where money moves fastest: 40 per cent of advertisers pay commission on programmatic buying, 5 per cent on offline planning. Palmer's model, a cut of the money passing through, is at its strongest in the newest channel: the ANA found 28 per cent paying a fixed-rate commission and 12 per cent a sliding scale on programmatic services, against 4 and 1 per cent on offline planning [22].. | Commission, sliding scale | 1 | 2 | 6 | 7 | 12 |
| Labor-based fee | 54 | 48 | 48 | 38 | 25 |
| Fixed fee (deliverables) | 24 | 25 | 23 | 21 | 18 |
| Value-based fee | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Media performance-based fee | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

### 1922. The first paid radio commercial

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/1922-the-first-radio-commercial/
Date: 2026-09-03. Read: 10 min.

On 28 August 1922 a property firm paid WEAF $50 to talk about apartments. What radio's first thirty years say about sponsoring a show versus buying the spot.

## The moment

Monday, 28 August 1922, a quarter past five in the afternoon. In the studio of AT&T's new station WEAF, on West Street in lower Manhattan, the announcer reads a short introduction. The radio audience "is to be addressed by Mr. Blackwell of the Queensboro Corporation", who "will say a few words concerning Nathaniel Hawthorne" [1]. Blackwell takes the slot. He talks about the novelist's ideals, about the "light shaft" that passes for daylight in a city apartment, about children "starved for a run over a patch of grass", and only near the end about the tenant-owned apartments his company has just named Hawthorne Court, in Jackson Heights, twenty minutes from Manhattan by subway. Queensboro has paid fifty dollars for the time. The script survives, which is more than any earlier paid broadcast can say.

## What came before

Radio in 1922 was a craze without a business model. Of the roughly 500 stations on the air that year, a quarter belonged to manufacturers and retailers and 40 per cent to schools, clubs, churches and government [9]. Performers worked for nothing. The question of who would pay hung over every studio.

Herbert Hoover, the commerce secretary who regulated the airwaves, rejected Britain's licence fee on the set and rejected advertising too. At the First National Radio Conference in February 1922 he said it was "inconceivable that we should allow so great a possibility for service, for news, for entertainment, for education, and for vital commercial purposes, to be drowned in advertising chatter" [7]. The conference recommended that direct advertising be prohibited outright.

AT&T had a different idea and the patents to try it. In February 1922 it announced what it called toll broadcasting: a station with no programmes of its own, a telephone booth to the air, where anyone could pay to speak. Printers' Ink, the print trade's paper, said the plan would prove "positively offensive to great numbers of people" [3]. The station opened as WBAY on 25 July, lost its signal among the skyscrapers, became WEAF in mid August, and waited twelve days for a customer.

WEAF was late to its own first. Frank Bremer is reported to have rented his amateur station in Jersey City to the Jersey Journal for a New Year's broadcast on the last night of 1921, for fifty dollars. WGI in Medford Hillside, Massachusetts, sold a programme to the Packard Motor Company of Boston on 4 April 1922, nearly five months before Hawthorne Court, and was stopped almost at once [2]. The record does not settle which came first. What WEAF has that the others lack is a script that survived, a company that kept its files, and a successor: AT&T sold the station in 1926 and it became the flagship of NBC.

## What it changed

The talk sold apartments. Fox records that Queensboro "quickly sold two apartments", and that by March 1923 the station had twenty-five sponsors, among them Macy's, Colgate and Metropolitan Life [4, p. 152]. Small money, and beside the point. For the first time a marketer could buy the attention of a household at a fixed hour, inside the home, with a human voice, and count what came back.

The audience came first.

The advertisers followed, and the money kept growing through the Depression. Hoover set the terms. At the Third Radio Conference in October 1924 he said that "the quickest way to kill broadcasting would be to use it for direct advertising", and the conference passed a resolution deprecating "the use of radio broadcasting for direct sales effort" [7][16]. So the early sponsors bought a name on a show rather than a sales pitch: the Eveready Hour, the A&P Gypsies, the Cliquot Club Eskimos [4, p. 153].

The networks made it national. NBC was formed by RCA on 25 September 1926 around the station it had bought from AT&T, and a rival that became CBS followed the next year [9]. Then Lord & Thomas put Amos 'n' Andy on NBC for Pepsodent and the serial became, in Fox's phrase, "the medium's first runaway success" [4, p. 156]. Wu's reading is that a sponsor had learned to "own" a part of the day, seven o'clock, every evening, across the country [5, p. 93].

Radio took its money from print. Newspapers carried 45 per cent of American advertising in 1935 and 32 per cent in 1945; radio went from 7 per cent to 15 [11].

The third change was a format. Procter & Gamble put a fifteen-minute serial called Ma Perkins on WLW in Cincinnati on 14 August 1933 and on NBC that December, to sell Oxydol [17]. Blackett-Sample-Hummert made the show, and it ran until 1960 [8, p. 358]. By 1937 Frank Hummert was the best-paid man in advertising, with a base salary of $132,000 [4, p. 160]. The soap opera was advertising with a programme wrapped round it, made by the agency and carried by the network.

## The Mad Men thread

In the series the agency writes thirty-second spots and a media man buys the time. The road there runs through radio. Through the 1930s and 1940s most sponsored network programmes were produced by advertising agencies: Kraft Music Hall by J. Walter Thompson, Cavalcade of America by BBDO for Du Pont, Show Boat by Benton & Bowles for Maxwell House, The Jack Benny Show by Young & Rubicam for General Foods [8, p. 355]. Blackett and Hummert had both trained at Lord & Thomas under Hopkins and Lasker, and they carried reason-why selling into the new medium. The agency was the studio. It held the time, hired the stars, wrote the scripts and folded the sponsor into the act, as Benny did every week in his opening greeting.

Television inherited the model and then broke it. Pat Weaver, who had produced Fred Allen's show at Young & Rubicam, joined NBC in 1949 with what he called the magazine plan: the network would own the programme and rent minutes inside it to several advertisers, as a magazine sells pages between articles. His memo that year reads, "There is not enough money to put on full programs for a single product" [8, p. 365].

Costs did the rest. The $64,000 Question, developed by Norman, Craig & Kummel and sold to Revlon, drew a 52.3 rating in the summer of 1955 and was, in Fox's words, "the last stronghold of independent production and single sponsorship" [4, p. 215]. The quiz scandals finished the form.

Television advertising went from $454 million in 1952, when most programmes had a single sponsor, to $1.6 billion in 1960, when most did not, and the agencies moved to making the commercials and buying the time, which Meyers notes paid them better than producing programmes [8, p. 366]. The agency in the series is what came out the other side: a creative department and a media department.

What the series leaves out is the lineage. Ogilvy, asked in 1958 to name his copy mentors, listed Hopkins, Hummert and Reeves [4, p. 238]. The man who ran the soap opera factory taught the man who wrote the Rolls-Royce ad.

## Applied: if you are a B2C brand

Say you sell a direct-to-consumer coffee subscription and a podcast with the right listeners offers you two deals. The 1930s deal is a year's outright sponsorship, your name in the title, the host reading for you in every episode. The 1960s deal is host-read spots bought by the episode, across that show and a dozen others.

The record says the sponsorship buys something the spot cannot. Oxydol stayed with Ma Perkins for twenty-three years and the show was called "Oxydol's Own" for most of them [17]. You get that only if you stay. Sponsors left anyway, for reasons that still apply. The programme cost more than the minutes. The brand was chained to one audience and one star. And once the arithmetic turned, one expensive minute in many shows beat thirty minutes in one.

Podcasting is walking the same road. In 2019 host-read ads were 66 per cent of United States podcast advertising revenue; in 2020 they were 56 per cent, as announcer-read and brand-supplied ads took share [14, p. 14]. Our view is that the first deal suits a brand with one product and a long horizon, and few others.

Sponsor if the show's listeners are your buyers, if you can commit for at least a year, if the host will fold you into the programme rather than interrupt it, and if every episode carries an offer you can count. If any of the four fails, buy spots across many shows, give each show its own code, and treat the first quarter as a test of which shows work.

## Applied: if you are a B2B brand

Say you run a logistics software company and a trade association offers you a sponsored webinar series: six sessions, their list, your logo. Before the price, ask who sets the agenda, who chooses the speakers, who keeps the registrant list, who holds the recording, and who has the slot next year. We put those five questions to clients before we look at a price.

If the association owns all of it, you are in AT&T's phone booth. You pay the toll, you speak, you leave, and the audience's loyalty stays with the station. It is a fair buy for reach, and it is what WEAF sold in 1922. If you set the agenda and book the speakers and the association supplies the room, you are the 1930s sponsor and its agency in one. It costs more and takes longer, and the identification is yours to keep.

Then apply the test the 1924 conference wrote down when it deprecated "direct sales effort" on the air [16]. If a session would be worth an hour of a freight manager's time with your name removed, it will carry your name. If it is a demonstration in disguise, the second session has an empty room. Blackwell spent his minutes on Hawthorne and the light shaft, and named the apartments last.

## What to do with it

1. Before any sponsorship, write down who owns the audience list, the recording, the editorial agenda and next year's slot. If the publisher owns all four, price it as a spot buy. 2. Put your name inside the programme or not at all: a title, a recurring segment, a host who uses the product on air. A logo on a slide is a spot at sponsorship prices. 3. Give every sponsored episode or session its own offer, code or landing page, and report what came back per episode. 4. Compare the two deals on cost per listener-minute, including your own production time; that cost is what moved television from sponsors to spots. 5. Fix the term, the renewal right and the fate of the archive in the contract. Sponsorships end; decide now whether the episodes stay up with your name on them.

### 1941. The first television commercial

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/1941-the-first-television-commercial/
Date: 2026-08-29. Read: 10 min.

The $9 Bulova spot of 1 July 1941 created the paid TV unit. Why it took thirty years, a scandal and a tobacco ban to become the 30-second spot you buy today.

## The moment

Tuesday, 1 July 1941, 2.29 in the afternoon. NBC's New York station, WNBT, is about to carry a ball game from Ebbets Field, the Brooklyn Dodgers against the Philadelphia Phillies. Before the first pitch, the few thousand sets in the city show a clock face over a map of the United States, and the station announcer, Ray Forrest, reads the line Bulova has paid for: "America runs on Bulova time." The bill is nine dollars, four for air time and five for station charges [5]. It runs about ten seconds. Then the ball game. That morning the Federal Communications Commission's new rules had come into force, and television, after a decade of experiments, was allowed to sell.

## What came before

Radio had already written the business model, and the unit of sale was the programme, whole. Advertisers, through their agencies, owned the shows outright. Sylvester "Pat" Weaver, who would later run NBC, began at Young and Rubicam making programmes for the agency's clients, because that is where programmes were made [9].

What held television back was the lack of an agreed technical standard. The National Television System Committee recommended 525 lines on 8 March 1941, the FCC approved it on 30 April and authorised commercial operation from 1 July, and on 2 May it licensed ten stations, WNBT holding licence number one [7].

Bulova's is called the first legal commercial because earlier experimental broadcasts had carried sponsor mentions nobody could be paid for. How long it ran is less settled than the date. Most accounts say ten seconds, others nine or twenty; Ad Age in 1995 described a "Bulova Time Check" with a ticking second hand, and the clock-over-a-map clip that circulates online is a reconstruction [5]. Then the war. From April 1942 to October 1945 the government halted production of new receivers, and in 1946, 8,000 American households owned a set.

## What it changed

On 2 July 1941 a marketer could buy seconds of attention, by the clock, in front of a moving picture with sound, inside the home. That unit, the paid spot, is what the Bulova bill records. For the next fifteen years almost nobody bought it that way.

Texaco Star Theater opened on NBC on 8 June 1948 with Milton Berle, when fewer than 2 percent of households had a set [8]. Households with television went from 172,000 in 1948 to 3.9 million in 1950, 30.7 million in 1955 and 52.7 million in 1965 [1].

Television advertising was $58 million in 1949, 1.1 percent of all US advertising. By 1954 it was $809 million and had passed radio and magazines; by 1960 it was $1.6 billion and 13.6 percent of the total, second only to newspapers [2].

But the thing being bought was still the programme. Most 1950s shows had a single underwriter, and, as the historian James Baughman puts it, "commercials and product plugs were routinely integrated into programs, including those for children" [12]. Weaver, now at NBC, set out to break that with the magazine concept: the network makes the programme and sells insertions to several advertisers, the way a magazine sells pages [9]. Today, from 14 January 1952, and Tonight, from 1954, were built as vehicles for it [10]. Erik Barnouw: "Now Weaver was determined that control should shift to the networks" [11].

The quiz shows took the programme from the sponsors. The $64,000 Question went on CBS on 7 June 1955 for Revlon; Twenty-One followed on NBC for Geritol. When Charles Van Doren told a House subcommittee on 2 November 1959 that he had been fed the answers, the hearings exposed producers and sponsors rigging outcomes, Congress made fixing a crime in 1960, and the networks took programme control for themselves [14][15]. From then on the sponsor was a buyer of time, and the agency's job on television was the spot.

The last change was the length of the unit. Through the 1960s the standard commercial was sixty seconds. The cigarette ban took tobacco off the air from 1 January 1971, the last spot running at 11.50 that night during Johnny Carson's programme, and tobacco had bought sixty-second units almost without exception [16]. The networks replaced the lost revenue by selling halves. The thirty-second spot became the standard.

Eighty-five years on, the unit survives and the pipe has changed. In May 2025 streaming took 44.8 percent of time spent with the television screen, more than broadcast and cable combined [25]. Connected television advertising was $9.7 billion in 2020 and $23.6 billion in 2024 [26].

## The Mad Men thread

The series runs from 1960 to 1970 inside a Madison Avenue agency, the years when the spot replaced the show.

Rosser Reeves at Ted Bates made the hard-sell spot the template. His Anacin commercial, hammers pounding inside a drawn skull and the promise of fast relief, was a fifty-nine-second film that cost $8,400; Reeves said Anacin came to Bates at $18 million a year in sales, went to $54 million within eighteen months, and spent $86 million putting that one film on the air [13]. His rule for the medium puts the decade in one sentence: "The purpose of a commercial is not to entertain the viewer but to sell him" [12].

Bill Bernbach at Doyle Dane Bernbach took the other road. Mark Tungate reads the industry as "this constant tug of war between two schools: the creatives, who believe art inspires consumers to buy, and the pragmatists, who sell based on facts" [17]. When DDB took Volkswagen to television it kept the print voice: one Beetle, one fact, a dry narrator, the 1964 "Snow Plow" spot asking how the man who drives the snowplough gets to the snowplough [23]. It is still the cleanest demonstration spot we know.

Leo Burnett in Chicago turned Marlboro into the cowboy in the mid-1950s, and on television the cowboy rode to the theme from The Magnificent Seven until the ban took him off the air [22].

David Ogilvy came to the medium late. The television chapter in Confessions of an Advertising Man, in 1963, is short and leans on borrowed research: commercials that set up a problem, "then prove the solution by demonstration, sell four times as many people as commercials which merely preach about the product" [18]. By 1983 he had rules of his own, ranking problem-solution, demonstration, testimonials and the derided talking head among the formats "found to be above average in their ability to change people's brand preference" [19]. Twenty years in, his rules and Reeves's had mostly converged; Ogilvy's just had better manners.

Stephen Fox opens The Mirror Makers with the medium's permanent reputation: "Practically everyone dislikes it. Advertising interrupts radio and television programs" [20]. The interruption was the business.

Two set pieces deserve the record. The series gives the Lucky Strike line "It's toasted" to its lead in 1960. American Tobacco's own history dates the first "IT'S TOASTED" newspaper ad to January 1917 and records that George Washington Hill retained Albert Lasker's Lord and Thomas late in 1925, eight years after the line [21]. The Kodak Carousel pitch is the series' invention: Kodak's timeline records the first Carousel projector in 1961, and its agency for most of the century was J. Walter Thompson [24].

## Applied: if you are a B2C brand

Say you sell a regional snack brand in four states and your media plan is social video and connected television. The record gives you one distinction, between attention you own and attention you rent. Most media plans we see at Brave New split the budget by channel and never by that line.

Texaco owned Tuesday night; when the audience arrived, it arrived for Texaco. That is what a creator series with your name on it, or your own channel, is today. You fund the programme, you carry a bad season, and the audience is yours for as long as you keep making it. The quiz scandals are the warning that comes with ownership. The moment the sponsor's thumb shows on the content, the audience leaves and the regulator arrives.

Connected television is the Bulova unit. You rent fifteen or thirty seconds in someone else's programme, and the record on how to spend them has not changed since Reeves and Ogilvy argued about it: one claim, one demonstration, the name early and often. The sixty-second spot died when the tobacco money left and the networks sold halves to fill the hole. So when a platform offers you six seconds, ask what the six replaces.

## Applied: if you are a B2B brand

Say you sell cybersecurity to mid-size banks and someone proposes a branded video series: a chief information security officer interviewing peers, your logo on the title card. Start where Weaver started, with control of the programme.

If you sponsor someone else's series, you are the 1950s advertiser without the 1950s power. You get the adjacency and they keep the editorial. If you make the series, you are NBC in 1952: you fund it, you set the format, and the audience, a few hundred security and risk officers at the banks you want, is yours for as long as the programme is worth their time.

The quiz-show lesson applies with more force here. Your buyers are paid to detect manipulation. A series in which every guest endorses your category, or every episode ends on your demo, is Twenty-One with the answers handed out in advance. Keep a wall between the people who sell and the people who book guests and cut episodes, and let a guest say something your sales team would rather they had not. It is the only reason the audience comes back.

Measure it by who returns for the second episode. Berle's audience in 1948 was tiny, and it bought the sets.

## What to do with it

1. Add an ownership column to the media plan. For every line, mark whether you own the programme or rent the time, what it costs to keep owning it next quarter, and what you lose if you stop. 2. Build the spot on one claim. State it in the first three seconds and demonstrate it once. Test the fifteen against the thirty on the same claim, and do not let the platform's default length decide. 3. If you fund a programme, write the Weaver rules before episode one: who sets the format, who books the guests, what the sponsor may never touch. Put them in the production contract. 4. Run a quiz-show audit on any series you already have. Count the episodes where the outcome favoured you. If it is all of them, your audience has noticed. 5. Price attention in Bulova units. Divide each channel's spend by the seconds of attention it bought, and compare owned programme with rented spot on the same line. Keep the one whose cost per second falls as the audience grows.

### 1960. The 4 Ps of marketing are published

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/1960-the-four-ps/
Date: 2026-08-24. Read: 10 min.

1960: McCarthy's four Ps and Levitt's Marketing Myopia turned marketing into a taught discipline, and left the agency holding one box out of four.

## The moment

Homewood, Illinois, 1960. The textbook publisher Richard D. Irwin brings out a 770-page volume by E. Jerome McCarthy called Basic Marketing: A Managerial Approach [1]. Inside, everything a marketing manager has to decide is sorted into four boxes that share a first letter: product, place, promotion, price.

The same summer, in Boston, the July to August issue of Harvard Business Review carries "Marketing Myopia" by Theodore Levitt, a lecturer in his second year at the Harvard Business School [2]. It opens by telling the railroads they were never in the railroad business. One book gives marketing a framework. One article gives it a question. Between them, the subject becomes something you can teach, examine, and be hired to run.

## What came before

The idea McCarthy compressed was already in the room. In 1948 James Culliton, in a Harvard research bulletin on manufacturers' marketing costs, had described the marketing executive as a "mixer of ingredients". His colleague Neil Borden built the term "marketing mix" on it, taught it for some fifteen years, and only wrote it up in 1964, by which time his list of ingredients ran to twelve, from product planning to "fact finding and analysis" [3]. Twelve ingredients will carry a case discussion. Four fit on an exam paper.

On the client side the job came even earlier. On 13 May 1931 a junior Procter and Gamble manager named Neil McElroy sent his boss a three-page memo asking for two more hires. It set out the duties of a "brand man": study shipments of his brands by units, study a weak territory "personally at first hand, both dealers and consumers", "take full responsibility for all other advertising expenditures" on his brands, and "experiment with and recommend wrapper revisions" [4]. That is product, place and promotion on one desk in Cincinnati, twenty-nine years before anyone alliterated them.

The market itself had changed shape. Richard Tedlow's history of American mass marketing runs in three phases: fragmentation, when nothing could travel far; unification, when the railroad and the telegraph let brands like Coca-Cola reach the whole country from the 1880s; and segmentation, which he dates to General Motors answering Ford's single Model T with "the car for every purse and purpose" in the 1920s [5]. A segmented market means more decisions, and more decisions is what a framework is for.

If you learned the four Ps from a Kotler textbook, Kotler is plain about where they came from: "I adopted these and helped popularize the 4Ps of Marketing" [6].

## What it changed

The money was already there. Total US advertising spending went from $5,700 million in 1950 to $11,960 million in 1960, a doubling in a decade [7]. As a share of the economy it reached 2.3 per cent of GDP in 1956 and again in 1960, then, in Galbi's series, drifted down to 1.9 per cent by 1970 [7]. The framework arrived at a high-water mark for advertising's weight in the economy, and put advertising in one box out of four.

What a marketer could do the day after was carry a structure around. A student could memorise four words, a professor could examine them, and a manager could write a plan with four headings. Master's degrees in business awarded in the United States went from 3,280 in 1955-56 to 6,874 in 1960-61 and 25,977 in 1970-71, an eightfold rise in fifteen years [8]. How many of those graduates sat a marketing paper, the table does not say. The ones who did arrived at an employer with the same four words.

Kotler started writing his own textbook in 1963; Prentice-Hall published Marketing Management: Analysis, Planning and Control in 1967, and professors told him they adopted it because "it raised respect for the marketing discipline" [6]. Fourteen editions later, Kotler and Keller still open with McCarthy, who "classified various marketing activities into marketing-mix tools of four broad kinds, which he called the four Ps of marketing", before proposing their own update of people, processes, programs and performance [9]. The framework has outlived its popularisers' attempts to replace it.

Levitt supplied the other half. The railroads, he wrote, "did not stop growing because the need for passenger and freight transportation declined. That grew." They were in trouble because they "assumed themselves to be in the railroad business rather than in the transportation business", which is to say "they were product oriented instead of customer oriented" [2]. The article won the McKinsey Award in 1960 [2] and has sold more than 850,000 reprints, which the Harvard Business School calls one of the best-selling HBR articles of all time [10]. HBR's editors later said it "introduced the most influential marketing idea of the past half-century: that businesses will do better in the end if they concentrate on meeting customers' needs rather than on selling products" [2].

Gartner's annual survey of chief marketing officers puts marketing budgets at 6.4 per cent of company revenue in 2021, 9.5 per cent in 2022, 9.1 per cent in 2023, 7.7 per cent in 2024 and 2025, and 7.8 per cent in 2026 [11, 12, 13, 14]. That is the modern mix, measured. In 2025, 39 per cent of CMOs planned to cut agency budgets [13].

At the company where the brand man was invented, advertising still runs at about a tenth of sales. Procter and Gamble's 10-K filings put advertising costs at $7.3 billion on net sales of $70,950 million in fiscal 2020 and $10.2 billion on $87,032 million in fiscal 2026, between 9.8 and 11.7 per cent in every year between [15, 16, 17].

## The Mad Men thread

The television series opens in 1960. The agencies its characters are modelled on were real. Rosser Reeves of Ted Bates, who built the "[unique selling proposition](/principles/unique-selling-proposition/)", had made the first spot commercials for a presidential candidate in 1952. In 1960 Marion Harper Jr. created Interpublic, the first agency holding company [18].

The series passes a Volkswagen advertisement around a conference table. The record is that the work was Doyle Dane Bernbach's, the agency Bernbach and Ned Doyle founded with Maxwell Dane in 1949, and that by October 1961 the New York Times described it as "widely recognized as one of this country's top creative agencies" [19, 20, 21].

David Ogilvy's shop, opened in 1948 as Hewitt, Ogilvy, Benson and Mather, went public in 1966 as Ogilvy and Mather, among the first agencies to do so [22]. Harper's holding company and Ogilvy's listing are the managerial revolution reaching the agencies.

So the Creative Revolution and the managerial revolution arrived in the same year. We read them as two different things. Daniel Pope reads the Creative Revolution as "a revolution in audience segmentation", in which advertisements "threw a knowing wink to the targeted customer group" expected to buy a Volkswagen [21]. That is Tedlow's third phase arriving on Madison Avenue. The agencies were getting better at the fourth P at the moment the client was handed a framework for all four.

The division of labour that followed has never been reversed. McCarthy's book gave the client a desk for each P. McElroy's brand man already sat at three of them. The agency's craft mapped onto one. The CMO Survey found in 2026 that marketing is primarily responsible for advertising in 86.9 per cent of US companies, for new products in 32.9 per cent, for pricing in 28.2 per cent and for distribution in 7.5 per cent [23]. Even inside the client, the fourth P is the one marketing reliably owns, and the one it buys from outside. The agency kept promotion in 1960. It has been defending that single box ever since.

## Applied: if you are a B2C brand

Say you are launching a beverage brand and the document you call the marketing plan is a media plan: channels, flights, a creative brief, a launch date. We see this plan a lot. It is one P written down and three assumed.

Start where McElroy's brand man started, with shipments by units. Which stores, which shelf, which temperature, which pack size. That is place, and "we are talking to a distributor" means you do not yet have one. Then product, meaning the format and the drinking occasion, which decide who you sit next to on the shelf and so what your price has to be. Then price, which is three prices: the shelf price, the retailer's margin, and the promotional price you will be asked for in month three. Only then promotion, and now the media plan has something to promote, a product in a place at a price.

If you are in the sparkling water business you compete on the shelf you chose. If you are in the afternoon-without-coffee business, the shelf, the price and the pack all move. Decide which before the creative brief is written, or the brief decides for you.

## Applied: if you are a B2B brand

Say you sell laboratory equipment and your marketing team reports to sales. The reporting line tells you which P the company thinks marketing is. Promotion, in service of a pipeline. It also means nobody owns Levitt's question.

Ask it in writing. Decide whether you are in the instruments business or the validated-results business. In the first, the four Ps are the box, the list price, the distributor network and the catalogue. In the second, the product includes consumables, calibration, the service contract and training; price can be per result or per month rather than per machine; place includes the laboratory's procurement portal and the tender; and promotion starts with the people who sign off a method, who are not the people who sign a purchase order. A marketing team that only ever briefs sales collateral is, in Levitt's phrase, product oriented instead of customer oriented, and it is so by design.

Write the one-sentence answer to "what business are we in", then write what each P means under that sentence. If marketing owns only one of the four, the plan should say which and why.

## What to do with it

1. Write down who sets each of the four Ps in your company, by name. If marketing sets fewer than three, call your plan a communications plan and budget it as one. 2. Before any media budget is approved, answer Levitt's question in one written sentence and have the person who owns product sign it. 3. Audit your last three marketing plans for the page count given to each P. Fewer than a page on place or on price is the finding. 4. Take the seven brand-man duties in McElroy's memo and assign each to a current job title. Any duty without an owner is a hole in your mix, and no agency brief will fill it. 5. Report marketing spend as a share of revenue every year, next to the Gartner average and your largest listed competitor's advertising-to-sales ratio, so the budget conversation starts from a number.
