Generative engine optimization, or GEO, is the practice of writing and structuring content so that generative engines cite it in the answers they produce. The term comes from a 2023 research paper by Pranjal Aggarwal and colleagues at Princeton, the Georgia Institute of Technology, the Allen Institute for AI and IIT Delhi.

## Who coined it, and what they actually measured

This is one of the few terms in [AI marketing](/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-marketing/) with a real paper behind it, so it is worth being precise about what the paper says.

Aggarwal and colleagues published "GEO: Generative Engine Optimization" in November 2023 [1]. They built a benchmark of around ten thousand queries and tested a set of content changes to see which ones increased a source's visibility inside a generated answer. The headline finding was that several simple changes produced measurable improvement, with the best performing ones reported as lifting visibility by up to around 40 per cent on their benchmark.

The methods that worked were not exotic. Adding citations to authoritative sources. Adding statistics. Adding direct quotations. In other words, the changes that make a page more useful to quote.

The methods that did not work are the more interesting half. Keyword stuffing, the central technique of two decades of search optimisation, did not help.

## Why the mechanism is different from SEO

Search optimisation competes for a position in a list. The page stays the page, and the reader clicks through to it.

Generative optimisation competes to be the material an answer is built from. The reader may never see your page. What they see is a sentence derived from it, possibly with your name attached and possibly not.

That changes what a good page looks like. A page built to rank is built to attract a click. A page built to be cited is built to be quotable: one claim per paragraph, stated plainly, with the source attached, in language that survives being lifted out of context. Those are not the same document.

## The honest limits

Three, and anyone selling GEO services should volunteer all three.

**The paper is one benchmark, from 2023.** Models have changed repeatedly since. A technique that lifted visibility on that benchmark may behave differently now, and almost nobody re-runs the test.

**Most GEO advice in circulation cites the paper without having read it.** The 40 per cent figure in particular travels detached from the conditions it was measured under, which is how a benchmark result becomes a sales claim.

**Retrieval does not always fire.** When we put eight marketing questions to a live engine with search grounding, it only retrieved for two of them. The rest were answered from the model's existing parameters, where no amount of page optimisation reaches. See [Research](/research/).

## What to do with it

1. Write one claim per paragraph and attach the source to the claim, not to the article. A paragraph that can be lifted intact is a paragraph that can be cited. 2. Put the answer in the first fifty words, before the context. That block is what gets extracted. 3. Use real numbers with dates and named sources. The paper found statistics and citations both improved visibility, and they are also just better writing. 4. Stop keyword stuffing. It did not work in the study and it makes the page worse to quote. 5. Check whether the engine is retrieving at all for your questions before investing in page changes. If it answers from memory, the work to do is different and slower.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

GEO is the most oversold term in this section, and it is oversold on the back of one real paper that most of the people quoting it have not read.

The thing worth knowing is that the techniques which worked in that study were all versions of "make the page genuinely more useful to quote". Citations, statistics, direct quotes. The technique that failed was the one the SEO industry spent twenty years selling. That should tell you how to judge a proposal: if it sounds like gaming, it is probably the thing that already stopped working.

Ask any supplier pitching GEO two questions. What does the engine currently say about us, and did they check whether it retrieves live for our questions at all. If the answer to the second is no, page-level work will not move it, and a proposal built on page-level work is a proposal built on a wrong assumption.

Sources:

1. Aggarwal, P., Murahari, V., Rajpurohit, T., Kalyan, A., Narasimhan, K. and Deshpande, A. (2023). GEO: Generative Engine Optimization. arXiv:2311.09735.

### What is answer engine optimization (AEO)?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-answer-engine-optimization/
Date: 2026-09-11. Read: 4 min.

Answer engine optimization, or AEO, is the practice of preparing content so that it is used in a direct answer rather than in a list of links. In practice it means answering one question per page, plainly and early, in a block that can be lifted out whole and still make sense.

## Where the term comes from, which is nowhere in particular

AEO has no founding paper. It is a trade term, and it predates the current wave of AI assistants: people were using it for featured snippets and voice search results years before a language model was involved.

That history is useful rather than embarrassing. The featured snippet era already established the core mechanic, which is that a page can win the answer and lose the visit. Everything happening now is a harder version of the same trade.

## How it differs from GEO, since the two are used interchangeably and should not be

They overlap, and the distinction is still worth holding.

**[GEO](/ai-marketing/what-is-generative-engine-optimization/)** is about being part of the material a generated answer is synthesised from, often alongside several other sources, with or without attribution.

**AEO** is about being the answer. One question, one page, one extractable block. It applies to featured snippets, voice assistants and AI overviews as much as to chat assistants.

In daily work the techniques converge. The reason to keep them apart is diagnostic: if your problem is that nobody cites you, that is a GEO problem. If your problem is that you are cited but the answer given is thin or wrong, that is an AEO problem, and the fix is in how your page is structured rather than in whether it is found.

## What an answer-shaped page looks like

Six things, none of them complicated.

The question is the heading, phrased the way a person would ask it rather than the way a marketer would title it. The answer is the first thing after it, in under about fifty words, before any context or qualification. One page answers one question. Headings are questions too, so that someone scanning gets the argument. Numbers carry their source and their date inline. And the page does not open by explaining what it is about to do.

That last one is the most commonly broken. A page that opens "in this article we will explore" has spent its extractable block on nothing.

## The uncomfortable trade

Winning the answer often means losing the visit. The reader gets what they came for and does not click.

Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling. The honest case for doing it anyway is that the alternative is not "they visit your site instead", it is "they get the answer from somebody else and never learn your name". Being the uncredited answer is bad. Being absent is worse. A named citation in an answer is worth more than it looks, because it reaches people at the moment they are deciding who knows what they are talking about.

That calculation changes by business. If your revenue depends on ad impressions on your own pages, losing the visit is a direct loss. If it depends on being known by people who will buy something considered and expensive later, it is mostly a gain.

## What to do with it

1. One question per page. If a page answers three, it will win none of them. 2. Put the answer first, under fifty words, before context. Write it so it survives being read alone. 3. Make every H2 a question somebody would actually type or say. 4. Attach dates to figures. An undated number is unusable in an answer and a careful engine will skip it. 5. Decide, deliberately, which pages you are willing to lose the click on. Not every page should be answer-shaped.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

There is a decision here that belongs to you rather than to marketing, and it is usually made by default.

Answer-shaped content trades traffic for presence. You will appear in more answers and get fewer visits. Whether that is a good trade depends entirely on how your business makes money, and nobody will ask you the question before reorganising the website around it.

If you sell something considered, expensive and infrequent, where buyers spend months forming a shortlist before they ever contact anyone, the trade is almost certainly worth it. Being the name that comes up when a buyer asks a neutral party is worth more than a session on your site that nobody can attribute to revenue anyway.

If your model depends on traffic to your own pages, it is a worse trade and should be made selectively, page by page.

Either way, make it once, explicitly, rather than discovering it a year later in a traffic report.

Sources:

1. Sharp, B. (2010). How Brands Grow: What Marketers Don't Know. Oxford University Press.

### What is AI SEO?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-seo/
Date: 2026-09-10. Read: 16 min.

AI SEO is the work of getting a company named, described correctly and cited in the answers that AI assistants and AI search features produce. It shares a base with search engine optimisation, a page a machine can reach and read, and adds the part that decides an answer: a plain definition, one description of the company repeated everywhere it appears, and claims an engine can attribute to a source.

On 14 September 2026 we asked one AI engine eight ordinary marketing questions and then checked every source it named. For six of the eight it never searched the web at all. Of the fifty-two URLs it listed, twenty-one return a 404. The engine was not lying on purpose. It was answering from memory, the way a confident person quotes a book they read years ago and misremembers the page.

That is the thing worth understanding before spending a pound on AI SEO. Sometimes the engine looks, and what you publish can enter the answer this month. Sometimes it does not look, and nothing you publish this year will move it. Knowing which of the two you are facing is most of the strategy.

Below: what AI SEO is, how an answer gets assembled, where generative engine optimization and answer engine optimization fit, what makes a brand retrievable, how to measure any of it, and the parts I would skip.

> Key takeaways > > AI SEO has two meanings. Using AI tools to do SEO faster is a workflow question. Getting into AI answers is the one that changes a pipeline. > > Engines do not always retrieve. In our 14 September 2026 study, live search fired on two of eight questions. On fresh, contested topics a new page can enter the answer within a cycle. On evergreen topics it cannot, at any quality. > > Verify anything an engine cites you. Twenty-one of fifty-two listed sources in that study did not exist. > > "AI SEO" is the biggest term in this cluster at 8,100 US searches a month, ahead of [AI marketing](/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-marketing/) at 5,400, generative engine optimization at 4,400 and answer engine optimization at 2,400 (Ubersuggest, 13 September 2026). > > third party sources do more work than your own site copy. An engine counts how many independent places describe you the same way.

## What AI SEO is, and how it differs from search engine optimisation

Search engine optimisation competes for a position on a list of ten links. AI SEO competes to be the sentence the model writes. The buyer sees one paragraph and two names, and the other eight are not seen at all.

The phrase itself carries two jobs, and people mix them constantly. The first is using AI tools inside the marketing team: clustering keywords, drafting, generating schema, mapping internal links. That saves hours and changes nothing about what a site deserves to be returned for. The second is optimising a site and a company's public record so that assistants and AI search features surface it. Both get called AI SEO. Only the second one decides whether a buyer hears your name.

Ranking eleventh used to cost traffic. Being missing from an answer costs the meeting. A company described three different ways across its own site, its listings and its press coverage is not pushed down a ranking by a model. It gets averaged into something vague, or dropped. That is the problem a [retrievable brand](/ai-marketing/what-is-a-retrievable-brand/) is built to solve, and it is a writing and record-keeping problem far more than a technical one.

The overlap with old-fashioned SEO is real at the base. Crawlable pages, clean site structure, legitimate coverage elsewhere. It separates above that. SEO is tuned to a query and a click. AI SEO is tuned to a category and a description.

## How an AI engine builds an answer

## First the retrieval

Before anything is written, the engine decides whether to search. If it does, it runs a handful of queries, pulls pages, and writes the answer with those pages in front of it. If it does not, it answers from what it absorbed in training, which is a compressed, undated memory of the web as it was when the model was built.

You can tell the difference from the outside. A grounded answer carries live citations. An ungrounded one carries confident source names that may or may not resolve.

## Then the writing

Once the material is in hand, the model writes a paragraph. It leans on whatever is easiest to lift: a plain definition, a heading that matches the question, a number with a source beside it, a named framework it can attribute to someone. Vague brand language gives it nothing to grip. This is the least mysterious part of AI SEO and the part most companies skip, because writing a flat definitional sentence about yourself feels beneath a brand team.

## The mini-story: an engine that invented twenty-one sources

Here is the study behind the number in the introduction. On 14 September 2026 we put eight questions to Gemini with Google Search grounding, one answer each, then requested every URL it named and recorded the status. Questions covered marketing principles, the history of advertising, neuromarketing, building a B2B brand for AI search, films and songs about advertising, whether a marketing encyclopedia exists, and the term retrievable brand.

Live retrieval fired twice. Both times it was a fresh, contested topic: AI search, and reference sites. The six evergreen questions were answered from memory, and that is where the dead URLs came from. Twenty-one of fifty-two listed sources returned not found or failed.

On the retrievable brand question, all sixteen grounded citations were real pages, and the mix was instructive. Two platform vendors, two trade publications, two software companies that use the word as a product name, seven small agency and consultant blogs, one Medium post. Small, recently published explainers sat beside the vendors. That is the opening. A new page on a contested topic can enter an answer inside an update cycle. The method and the full table are in [our citation study](/research/how-ai-engines-answer-marketing-questions/), including the limits: one engine, one sample per question.

[VIDEO: a talk or explainer on how AI search assembles answers; Anne to choose]

## Generative engine optimization and answer engine optimization

Two named practices sit inside AI SEO. They are used almost interchangeably now, and the work behind them is the same work.

## GEO

[Generative engine optimization](/ai-marketing/what-is-generative-engine-optimization/), or GEO, is the practice of writing and structuring content so that generative engines cite it in the answers they produce. The term comes from a paper posted to arXiv in November 2023 by Pranjal Aggarwal, Vishvak Murahari, Tanmay Rajpurohit, Ashwin Kalyan, Karthik Narasimhan and Ameet Deshpande. You can read [the GEO paper on arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735). It introduced the term and a benchmark for testing which changes to a source make it more likely to be used in a generated answer, and the authors reported visibility gains of up to 40 per cent on that benchmark.

The practical reading: a generative engine is not ranking pages for a click. It is assembling an answer and choosing which sources to lean on. Content that states a claim plainly, attributes it, and puts a quotable sentence next to a source gives the engine something to reuse.

## AEO

[Answer engine optimization](/ai-marketing/what-is-answer-engine-optimization/), or AEO, is the practice of preparing content so it is used in a direct answer rather than a list of links. In practice it means answering one question per page, plainly and early.

AEO grew out of the years when search engines started answering questions on the results page itself through featured snippets and knowledge panels. The habit that built, one question and one clear answer per page, transferred straight to AI assistants. The mechanics are dull. Use the question as the heading, in the words people type. Answer it in the first two or three sentences. Keep the answer self-contained so it still makes sense when it is lifted out of the page. Put a date, an author and a source on it.

Where people separate the two terms, AEO is about the direct answer and GEO about the generated one. Search demand tells you which name to use rather than which practice to run. "AI SEO" measures 8,100 US searches a month, generative engine optimization 4,400, answer engine optimization 2,400 (Ubersuggest, 13 September 2026), and the AEO phrasing is the one climbing: "what is answer engine optimization" went from 210 a month in August 2025 to 2,400 by July 2026. We tracked all three lines in [how the AI search vocabulary moved](/research/how-the-ai-search-vocabulary-moved/).

## Retrievability, and the retrievable brand

Retrievability is not a marketing invention. It comes from information retrieval, the research field behind search engines, where Leif Azzopardi and Vishwa Vinay proposed it in 2008 as a measure of how easily a document can be surfaced by a retrieval system. Applied to a company it asks something blunter: when a buyer asks for the category, does the name come back.

A retrievable brand is one that AI assistants and search engines can find, name and describe correctly when a buyer asks a question. It is built from clear definitions, named frameworks, sourced facts and consistent descriptions repeated across every public source a model reads. Brave New, which publishes the Hive, uses [retrievable brand](https://brave-new.com/retrievable-brand/) as the name of its method, and that page carries the pillars and the measurement in full.

## The mini-story: what a brand does inside a head

In 2004, Samuel McClure and colleagues published a study in Neuron, from Read Montague's lab at Baylor College of Medicine. People drank Coke and Pepsi inside an fMRI scanner, blind and then labelled. Blind, preferences split. With the Coke label visible, stated preference shifted towards Coke and brain activity changed in regions associated with memory and self-image. The [Coke and Pepsi study](/branding/the-coke-pepsi-study/) is the most cited demonstration that a brand is a stored pattern in the buyer rather than a property of the product.

I keep coming back to it because AI SEO is the same idea with a second head to fill. The brand has always lived as an association in a person. Now there is a second store of associations, assembled from public text, and a buyer consults it before they consult themselves. What is written about you is what gets stored, and most brand budgets are still aimed at the first head.

This is also why a rebrand costs more than it used to. The old description stays on the web, and it keeps being counted. Models do not retire your previous positioning because you did.

## The machine-readable layer

Schema markup tells a machine what a page is rather than making it guess. [Schema.org](https://schema.org/) has the vocabulary. For AI SEO the useful types are Organization, Article, FAQPage, and DefinedTerm for anything you are defining. Put the same company description inside the Organization markup that you use on the About page, word for word.

[llms.txt](/ai-marketing/what-is-llms-txt/) is a plain text file at the root of a site that gives AI systems a short, curated summary and links to the pages worth reading. Jeremy Howard of Answer.AI [proposed it in 2024](https://llmstxt.org/). It is a convention, not a standard, and no provider is obliged to read it. It takes about an hour. The honest benefit is a side effect: writing one forces a company to say plainly what it does and which pages matter.

The third piece is the one people ignore because it is boring. One entity statement, a sentence or two saying what the company is, who it serves and where, repeated without variation on the site, in the schema, in every directory, every profile, every author bio, every partner page. Marketers resist this because repeating the same sentence feels lazy. It is the opposite. Variation is the part the writer enjoys and the part the machine cannot use, which is an uncomfortable trade if you came up through copywriting. There is a whole entry on [why brand consistency matters for AI search](/ai-marketing/why-brand-consistency-matters-for-ai-search/) if you want the argument in full.

## How to measure AI SEO

By asking the engines and counting. There is no dashboard handed down from the providers, and anyone selling certainty about the weighting is guessing.

Write the ten questions a buyer would actually type. Not your keywords. The awkward, specific phrasing a procurement lead uses at eleven at night. Ask each engine you care about, and record three things per answer: whether you are named, where in the answer you appear, and whether the description matches what you say about yourself. That is the baseline and it takes an afternoon.

Take the same count against named competitors, in the same prompts, on the same day. A number with nothing beside it means nothing. Then log every source the answers cite, because those pages are the ones shaping your category, and being described correctly on them moves an answer more than another post on your own blog. [How models choose which brands to recommend](/ai-marketing/how-ai-models-choose-brands/) goes further into that mechanism.

Repeat quarterly. Answers move as the sources move, and one reading tells you nothing about direction. And verify every citation before you repeat it, for the reason the study above made plain.

## What not to do

Do not pay for volume. Publishing forty thin posts a month to feed the machine produces forty pages nothing wants to quote. The pages that got cited in our study were definition-first explainers with question headings and a visible date.

Do not buy a tool before you have a baseline. The afternoon of manual checks tells you more than a subscription, and it tells you whether the engines are even retrieving on your topics.

And I would not chase the term. AI SEO, GEO, AEO, LLM optimisation: the names have churned every few months while the work underneath them has not changed. Pick one category you intend to be returned for and defend it on every surface, which is [positioning](/principles/positioning-in-marketing/) with a new set of readers.

## The mini-story: the first banner ad

On 27 October 1994, HotWired ran a banner for AT&T. It asked whether the reader had ever clicked their mouse right here, and told them they would. Click-through rates for that first campaign are widely reported as far above anything the format managed afterwards.

[The first banner ad](/history-of-advertising/1994-the-first-banner-ad/) is worth remembering for the shape of what followed. A new channel opens, the first movers get results that look like a law of nature, the numbers decay as everyone arrives, and what survives is whatever was a genuine asset rather than a trick of novelty. AI answers are somewhere in the early part of that curve. The tricks that work this quarter will be priced out by next year. A clear definition of what your company is, sourced and repeated, will still be doing work in five.

## Frequently asked questions

## Is AI SEO the same as SEO?

They share a base and separate at the goal. Both need pages a machine can reach and read, a clean structure and real coverage elsewhere. SEO competes for a position on a list of links, while AI SEO competes to be named inside a written answer.

## How do I get my company mentioned in ChatGPT?

Publish a plain definition of what you do, keep that description identical everywhere it appears, and earn coverage on the sources the engines already cite for your category. Then check the answers monthly and record whether you are named and whether the description is right.

## Does llms.txt actually work?

It is a proposed convention rather than a standard, and no model provider is required to read it. It costs about an hour, so the downside is small. The reliable benefit is that writing one forces you to state plainly what your site is and which pages matter.

## How long does AI SEO take to show results?

It depends entirely on whether engines retrieve live pages for your topic. On fresh, contested subjects a new page can appear in answers within an update cycle. On settled evergreen topics the engine answers from training data, and nothing you publish moves it in the near term.

## Can I pay to appear in AI answers?

Not directly, in the way you buy a search ad. What you can pay for is the work underneath: research worth citing, coverage on sources the engines already use, and a site clean enough to read. Anyone promising guaranteed placement in an assistant's answer is selling something they do not control.

## The short version

AI SEO is not a new discipline so much as an old one with a different reader. The reader is a machine assembling a paragraph, and it rewards what careful human readers have always rewarded: a plain statement of what you are, made early, made once, repeated without variation, with a source next to every number.

Start with the count. Ten questions a buyer would type, run against the engines your buyers use, recorded against named competitors on the same day. You will learn in one afternoon whether the engines retrieve on your topics at all, which decides whether publishing is a strategy or a waste. Then fix the entity statement everywhere it appears, which is unglamorous and finite work that most companies have never done.

Everything else is sequencing. The vocabulary will change again. Two years ago none of these terms existed, and the study that produced the numbers in this piece will need repeating on other engines before I would call any of it settled.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

AI SEO is the broadest term in this section and the one most likely to arrive as a proposal with a number attached. Three questions keep that conversation honest.

**What do the engines say about us now, with today's date on it.** If nobody recorded the starting point, nobody can show you movement later, and you will be shown activity instead. This costs nothing and takes ten minutes.

**Does the engine look things up for our buyers' questions, or answer from memory.** These need different work on different timescales. A plan built on page rewrites is addressed to the first case only, and in our own testing the engine retrieved for two questions out of eight.

**Is our problem absence, confusion, or an out-of-date description.** They look the same from a dashboard and they are not the same job. Confusion is the most urgent, because a confident wrong answer is being repeated to everyone who asks, and it is the one nobody notices.

What I would not do is treat this as a new discipline requiring a new budget line before those three answers exist. Most of what moves the needle here is the same work that made companies well known before any of this: being described accurately, in the same words, by people who are not you.

Sources:

1. Aggarwal, P., Murahari, V., Rajpurohit, T., Kalyan, A., Narasimhan, K. and Deshpande, A. (2023). GEO: Generative Engine Optimization. arXiv:2311.09735.
2. Azzopardi, L. and Vinay, V. (2008). Retrievability: an evaluation measure for higher order information access tasks. Proceedings of the 17th ACM Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM).
3. Lewis, P., Perez, E., Piktus, A. et al. (2020). Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks. arXiv:2005.11401. NeurIPS 2020.
4. Howard, J. (2024). The llms.txt proposal, Answer.AI, September 2024, llmstxt.org. A proposal rather than a ratified standard; adoption by the major AI companies remains limited.
5. Sharp, B. (2010). How Brands Grow: What Marketers Don't Know. Oxford University Press.

### What is a retrievable brand?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-a-retrievable-brand/
Date: 2026-09-08. Read: 5 min.

A retrievable brand is one an AI system can find, identify correctly and describe accurately when somebody asks about its category. Three conditions, and all three have to hold: the system has encountered you, it knows which entity you are, and what it says about you is true.

## Where the word comes from, and what we have done with it

Retrievability is not our term. It comes from information retrieval research, where Leif Azzopardi and Vishwa Vinay proposed retrievability in 2008 as a measure of how easily a document in a collection can be found by the queries a system is likely to receive [1]. It was a property of documents in an index, not a marketing idea.

Brave New uses it as the name for a method, applied to companies rather than documents. That is an adaptation, and it should be labelled as one rather than presented as established literature. The underlying insight carries over cleanly: in any collection, some items are structurally easy to surface and others are structurally hard, and that property can be measured and improved independently of quality.

## The three conditions, in the order they fail

**Presence.** Has the system encountered you at all. A company that exists only on its own website, with no third party mention, is close to invisible to a model trained on the open web. This is the most common failure and the slowest to fix, because the remedy is other people writing about you.

**Identity.** Does the system know which entity you are. Companies that share a name with another company, a product, or a common phrase get merged. The system answers confidently about a composite that does not exist. This is the failure that produces the strangest results and the one most likely to go unnoticed.

**Accuracy.** Is the description right. A system can know exactly who you are and still describe you by what you did five years ago, or by the one service that happens to be best documented on the open web rather than the one that makes your money.

Most work sold as AI visibility addresses the first and ignores the second and third. The order matters, because improving presence while identity is broken just produces more confident wrong answers.

## Why it is not the same as ranking

Ranking is comparative and positional. Retrievability is binary and then qualitative: can you be found, and once found, is the account of you correct.

A brand can be highly retrievable and never recommended, because the model knows exactly who you are and judges you a poor fit. That is a positioning problem and no amount of technical work will fix it. A brand can also be recommended while badly described, which is worse than it sounds, because every recommendation carries the error with it.

Separating the two is the point of the concept. They have different causes and different remedies.

## What makes a brand retrievable

Consistency, mostly, which is unglamorous.

The same entity name spelled the same way everywhere. A single canonical description that does not drift between the website, the directory listings, the founder's profiles and the press. third party sources that corroborate what you say about yourself, because a model weighs independent mention differently from self-description. Structured data that states plainly what the company is. And enough published material in your own category that there is something to retrieve.

None of that is a trick. It is the machine-readable version of being a coherent company, which is why brands with confused positioning tend to be badly described by AI as well as by people.

## What to do with it

1. Test all three conditions separately. Ask an engine who you are, what you do, and who it would recommend in your category. Three different questions. 2. If identity is confused, fix that before anything else. Disambiguate the name, the location and the category in every place you control. 3. Write one canonical description of the company and use it verbatim everywhere. Not a version per channel. 4. Count your third party mentions. If every source about you is published by you, presence is the constraint. 5. Re-test quarterly and keep the dates. Answers drift, and an undated test tells you nothing about direction.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The failure that should worry you is not absence. It is confident misdescription, because it is invisible from the inside and it compounds.

If an assistant has merged you with a similarly named company, or is describing a service you stopped offering, it is telling that to every person who asks, identically, with no indication that it is unsure. You will not see it in any dashboard. Nobody will email to tell you. The first signal is usually a prospect arriving with a wrong idea of what you do, and that gets filed as a bad lead rather than as a symptom.

Ask three questions yourself, by name, in one sitting. Who is [your company]. What does [your company] do. Who would you recommend for [your category].

If the first two come back wrong, that is a correction project and it is urgent. If they come back right and the third does not name you, that is a positioning problem and no technical fix will touch it.

Sources:

1. Azzopardi, L. and Vinay, V. (2008). Retrievability: an evaluation measure for higher order information access tasks. Proceedings of the 17th ACM Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM).

### How do AI models choose which brands to recommend?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/how-ai-models-choose-brands/
Date: 2026-09-06. Read: 4 min.

Two different mechanisms, and which one is running decides what you can do about it. Either the model answers from what it absorbed during training, or it searches the live web first and builds an answer from what it finds. The first is slow to influence and the second is fast, and most advice in circulation assumes the second without checking.

## The two paths

This is not a marketing observation. It is the architecture, and it has a paper. Patrick Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI Research, University College London and New York University set out retrieval-augmented generation in 2020: a model that combines what it learned in training with documents fetched at the moment of answering [1]. Every assistant a buyer uses is some version of that design.

Which means the question "how does the model choose brands" has two answers, depending on which half is doing the work.

**From parameters.** The model answers from patterns in its training data. No retrieval happens. Which brands appear depends on how often and how consistently they were described across the open web at training time. You cannot edit this. You can only change what gets written about you, and wait for the next training run.

**From retrieval.** The model runs a search, reads results, and synthesises an answer from them, usually with citations. Here page-level work matters immediately, and this is the path that [GEO](/ai-marketing/what-is-generative-engine-optimization/) addresses.

The commercially important point is that you do not get to choose which path runs. The engine decides, per question, and it does not tell you.

## When retrieval actually fires

We tested this rather than assuming it. In September 2026 we put eight marketing questions to a live engine with search grounding and checked, for each one, whether it retrieved.

It retrieved for two. The other six were answered from the model's existing knowledge, with no search performed. The pattern was consistent: questions about current AI search topics and about reference sites triggered retrieval, while evergreen questions about principles, history and theory did not.

That has a direct consequence. For a category where buyers ask evergreen questions, optimising pages will not move the answer, because no page is being read. The work is slower and sits upstream: getting described, accurately and repeatedly, in sources that will be in the next training set.

Full method and the date in [Research](/research/).

## What the model is actually weighing

Honestly: nobody outside the labs knows precisely, and anyone claiming a ranking formula is inventing it.

What can be observed is directional. Brands mentioned often across many independent sources appear more readily than brands mentioned rarely or only on their own site. Brands described consistently appear with more confident descriptions. Brands whose name is ambiguous get merged with whatever shares the name. And in retrieval mode, sources that are easy to quote, with a clear claim and an attached source, get used more than sources that bury the point.

That is a weaker statement than most of the industry makes, and it is the honest one.

## The citation problem nobody mentions

When we checked every source the engine named across those eight questions, of 52 URLs, 17 existed, 14 blocked automated checking, and 21 did not exist at all.

Roughly two in five of the sources it cited were not real. They looked plausible: correct domains, sensible paths, titles that fit the claim. They simply were not there.

That is worth holding onto when you read a report showing your brand cited in AI answers. Some of those citations may point at pages that have never existed, including on your own domain.

## What to do with it

1. Establish which path runs for your category before buying anything. Ask the question, see whether it cites sources, and record the date. 2. If it retrieves, page-level work pays and you should do it. 3. If it does not retrieve, stop optimising pages for it. Invest in third party mention, directories, reference sites and anywhere your category gets written about by people who are not you. 4. Verify any citation report you are shown. Click the URLs. 5. Re-test quarterly. Engines change retrieval behaviour without announcing it.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

Before approving any budget here, make someone answer one question: does the engine actually look things up when our buyers ask, or does it answer from memory.

It is a cheap test and it determines whether the entire proposal in front of you is addressed to the right mechanism. If the engine is not retrieving for your category, a programme of page rewrites will produce reports full of activity and no change in what buyers are told.

The second thing to insist on, if anyone shows you a dashboard of AI citations: click some of them. We found two in five of the sources an engine named did not exist. A citation report is not evidence until somebody has checked that the pages are real.

Sources:

1. Lewis, P., Perez, E., Piktus, A., Petroni, F., Karpukhin, V., Goyal, N., Kuttler, H., Lewis, M., Yih, W., Rocktaschel, T., Riedel, S. and Kiela, D. (2020). Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks. arXiv:2005.11401. Accepted at NeurIPS 2020.

### How do I get my company mentioned in ChatGPT and Perplexity answers?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/get-mentioned-in-chatgpt-and-perplexity/
Date: 2026-09-04. Read: 4 min.

By being described, accurately and repeatedly, in sources the engines use, and by making sure the engine knows which company you are. There is no submission form, no paid placement in the answer itself, and no technical switch. Anyone offering guaranteed inclusion is describing something that does not exist.

## Start by checking what happens now

Before anything else, run three questions and write down the answers with the date.

Ask who your company is. Ask what it does. Ask who it would recommend in your category and city or sector. Do it in both engines, because they behave differently: Perplexity retrieves aggressively and cites, while ChatGPT varies by question and by mode.

Most of what gets sold as an AI visibility programme skips this step, which is how companies end up paying to improve a presence they already had, or optimising pages for an engine that is not reading pages.

## The two levers, in order of difficulty

**Third party mention.** The single biggest factor, and the slowest. Engines weigh what others say about you differently from what you say about yourself. A company covered in trade press, listed in sector directories, cited in industry reports and quoted by name has material to be retrieved. A company whose only footprint is its own site does not.

This is unglamorous, it is mostly public relations and partnerships, and it is the thing that actually moves. It is also why the brands that AI names confidently tend to be the ones that were already well known.

**Your own published material.** Faster, and it only pays when the engine is retrieving. One question per page, answered in the first fifty words, with sources attached to claims. See [What is answer engine optimization?](/ai-marketing/what-is-answer-engine-optimization/). Whether this works at all for your category depends on [which path the engine is running](/ai-marketing/how-ai-models-choose-brands/).

## The things that do not work

Keyword stuffing. It did not help in the one controlled study we have on generative visibility, and it makes a page worse to quote.

Writing pages that assert your own excellence. Engines synthesise from many sources and a self-congratulatory page is low-value material to quote from. A page that states a verifiable fact about your work is worth more than a page that states you are a leader.

Any vendor guaranteeing placement. There is no inventory to buy. Sponsored placement around AI answers exists in some products and is a different thing, labelled as advertising, and it does not make the model recommend you.

## A realistic timeline

Fast, in weeks: fixing a wrong description where you control the source, disambiguating your name, adding structured data, restructuring key pages.

Slow, in quarters: building enough independent mention that a model answering from training data has something to draw on. This is a public relations timeline, not a content timeline, and it does not compress with budget as readily as people expect.

Anyone promising a change in how a model describes you within a month is either talking only about the retrieval path, or not being straight with you.

## What to do with it

1. Run the three questions in both engines. Record answers and dates. 2. Fix identity first if the engine has you confused with another entity. Everything downstream is wasted until that is right. 3. Write one canonical company description and use it verbatim everywhere. 4. Build third party mention deliberately: trade press, sector directories, industry reports, conference listings, partner sites. 5. Make your own key pages answer-shaped, but only after establishing that the engine retrieves for your category. 6. Re-run the three questions quarterly, same wording, and keep the log. The log is the only evidence of direction you will have.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The honest summary is that getting mentioned in AI answers is mostly the same work as becoming well known, which you already knew how to do, running on a longer timeline than anybody selling it will admit.

Two things protect you here. First, insist on the before picture with a date on it. If nobody recorded what the engines said in month zero, nobody can prove anything changed in month six, and you will be shown activity metrics instead.

Second, be suspicious of speed. The lever that genuinely moves this is other people writing about you, which is a public relations timeline measured in quarters. A proposal promising to change how a model describes your company in a month is either describing a much smaller thing than it sounds, or it is not true.

The cheapest useful action available to you today costs nothing: ask both engines who you are, and find out whether the problem is absence, confusion, or a description that is simply out of date.

### What is llms.txt?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-llms-txt/
Date: 2026-09-03. Read: 3 min.

A proposed standard: a plain markdown file at the root of a website, /llms.txt, giving language models a curated guide to what the site contains and which pages matter. It was proposed by Jeremy Howard of Answer.AI in September 2024. It is a proposal, not a ratified standard, and adoption by the major AI companies is limited.

## What it is for

The argument behind it is reasonable. A language model reading a website has a limited context window and encounters a lot of noise: navigation, cookie banners, boilerplate, duplicated template text. A curated file that says here is what this site is, here are the pages that matter, here is what each one covers, makes the site cheaper and more accurate to read.

It is deliberately similar in spirit to `robots.txt`, which tells crawlers what they may access, and to a sitemap, which tells them what exists. The difference is that `llms.txt` is meant to tell them what is worth reading and what it means.

The format is markdown rather than XML, on the reasoning that models read markdown well and humans can maintain it.

## The part that gets left out of most articles about it

Adoption is the whole question, and it is usually skipped.

A proposal only works if the systems it addresses honour it. As of now, the major AI companies have not committed to reading `llms.txt` in the way search engines committed to `robots.txt` decades ago. A number of developer-tooling companies publish one. That is not the same as the engines consuming it.

So the honest position is this. Publishing `llms.txt` is cheap, harmless, and may help if adoption arrives. Treating it as a lever that will change how AI describes your company today is not supported by anything observable.

If you see a service charging meaningfully for `llms.txt` implementation, the work involved is writing a short markdown file. Price it accordingly.

## What one looks like

A heading with the site name. A short blockquote summarising what the site is. Then sections of markdown links, each with a one-line description of what the page covers, grouped so the important material is first and optional material is under a section marked optional.

That is the whole format. It is intentionally simple.

## What to do with it

1. Publish one if you have a content-heavy site. It takes an hour and it costs nothing to maintain if you keep it short. 2. Write the descriptions for a reader who knows nothing about you. The value is in the one-line summaries, not in the links. 3. Do not pay a meaningful sum for it, and do not let it displace work that is evidenced. 4. Keep it current. A stale guide is worse than none, because it misdescribes. 5. Check back on adoption periodically rather than assuming either way.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

This is a small item that occasionally appears in proposals with a price attached that does not match the work.

`llms.txt` is a text file. Writing a good one for a normal company website is an hour, maybe two if the descriptions are written carefully. It may turn out to matter and it may not, because the companies it is addressed to have not committed to reading it.

Publish one. Spend an hour on it. Then put your attention on the things that are evidenced: whether the engines describe you correctly, and whether anybody other than you has written about your company.

If a line item for AI file standards appears in a scope of work at a few thousand, ask what else is in it.

### Why does brand consistency matter for AI search?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/why-brand-consistency-matters-for-ai-search/
Date: 2026-09-01. Read: 5 min.

Because an AI system builds its account of your company by aggregating everything it has seen about you, and inconsistency does not average out into a blurry picture. It produces either a confident wrong answer or a merged entity that is partly you and partly somebody else.

## The mechanism, which is different from the human one

A person reading three slightly different descriptions of your company understands them as three descriptions of one company. They resolve the difference without noticing.

A retrieval system does not necessarily do that. It is matching strings and embeddings. If your company appears as one name on the website, a slightly different legal name in a directory, an abbreviation on the founder's profile and a former name in older coverage, the system may treat those as related or may not. When it does not, your evidence is split across several partial entities, none of which has enough weight to be recommended.

This is the quiet cost of inconsistency, and it is invisible in every conventional marketing metric. Nothing in your analytics will show it.

The problem has a name and a literature older than the web. Ivan Fellegi and Alan Sunter published a formal theory of record linkage in 1969, working out how a system should decide whether two records refer to the same entity when the fields disagree [1]. Their answer, in essence, is that the decision is probabilistic and that agreement on rare values counts for far more than agreement on common ones.

Apply that to a company. A distinctive name spelled identically everywhere is a rare value and links your records together strongly. A generic descriptor shared with four hundred other firms is a common value and links almost nothing. This is why an unusual, consistently spelled name is worth more to a machine than a descriptive one, which is close to the opposite of what most naming advice says.

## Where consistency actually has to hold

Five places, and the first is the one most often broken.

**The entity name.** One spelling, everywhere. Trading name, legal name and abbreviation are three different strings. Pick which one is the public entity and use it without variation.

**The category description.** What you do, in the same words, on the website, in directories, in profiles and in press. Not a bespoke version per channel.

**Location and region.** Companies operating across several markets often list different primary locations in different places and get read as different firms.

**The people.** A founder whose title varies across profiles weakens the link between person and company, and that link is one of the strongest signals connecting scattered mentions.

**The claims.** If the site says one thing about scope and the proposals say another, the retrievable description will be the one that appears in more places, which is usually not the one you would choose.

## Why this is a strategy problem wearing a technical costume

Companies with confused positioning are described inconsistently because they describe themselves inconsistently, and they do that because nobody has settled what the company is.

You see it most in firms that do several things for several audiences. Each channel gets copy written for its own audience, each is reasonable on its own, and the aggregate is incoherent. The AI description of such a company is not wrong so much as it is an average of contradictions.

Fixing that is not a technical task. It is deciding what the company is, which is an argument that has usually been avoided for years because it is easier to add another audience than to choose.

## What to do with it

1. Write down every place your company is described: site, directories, profiles, press, partner pages, event listings. It will be longer than you expect. 2. Pick one canonical name string and one canonical description. Decide once. 3. Correct the list, starting with the sources you do not control, since those carry more weight and take longer. 4. Give the founder and senior people identical titles and company references across profiles. 5. Add structured data stating the entity plainly. 6. Re-check quarterly. Drift is the normal state; consistency is maintained, not achieved.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

This is the entry in this section that is really about you rather than about marketing.

An AI system describes your company inconsistently when your company describes itself inconsistently, and that almost always traces back to a decision nobody has been willing to make. Usually it is the question of what you actually do, left open because closing it means telling an audience, a service line or a market that they are no longer the priority.

The useful thing about AI search is that it makes the cost visible. A buyer asking an assistant about your category gets one description of you, and if your company has three positions, the description will be the mushiest of the three.

The work is a morning: decide the name, decide the one-sentence description, decide the primary market. Then the rest is administration, and it can be delegated.

What cannot be delegated is the deciding. If the last three people who tried to write the company description came back asking you to choose, that is the signal, and the AI problem is a symptom rather than the thing to fix.

Sources:

1. Fellegi, I. P. and Sunter, A. B. (1969). A Theory for Record Linkage. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 64(328), 1183 to 1210.

## 05 Reputation

What a reputation is, how it differs from a brand, how trust is measured, and what the documented cases teach about keeping it.

### Brand versus reputation: what is the difference?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/brand-versus-reputation/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 4 min.

A brand is what a company says and shows about itself. A reputation is what other people conclude from what it does. One is authored, the other is earned, and in a buying meeting the second one decides.

## Why the distinction is worth holding

Most writing treats the two as synonyms, which is why so much money gets spent on the wrong one.

The useful test is ownership. You own your brand: the name, the identity, the positioning, the claims. You do not own your reputation. It lives in other people's heads and in what they say when you are not in the room. You can influence it, slowly, by what you do. You cannot edit it.

Charles Fombrun, who did more than anyone to make corporate reputation a measurable field, defined it as a collective assessment built up over time from a company's past actions and its prospects for the future [1]. The two load bearing words are collective and past. It is other people's verdict, and it is retrospective.

## Where each one actually operates

**Brand does the early work.** Getting known, getting recognised, getting into the consideration set. That is mental availability and it is well evidenced [2]. A brand that nobody can recall is not in the running, whatever its reputation.

**Reputation does the late work.** Once a buyer is comparing two credible options, the question stops being who are you and becomes what happens if I choose you and it goes wrong. That is a reputation question and no amount of identity work answers it.

Which is why the two fail differently. Weak brand, strong reputation: you are excellent and nobody shortlists you. Strong brand, weak reputation: you get shortlisted constantly and lose at the last stage, usually without being told why.

The second failure is more expensive and much harder to see, because the pipeline looks healthy right up to the point it does not close.

## The asymmetry

Reputation is built slowly and lost quickly, and the asymmetry is not sentimental, it is structural. Evidence that confirms a good reputation arrives as ordinary competence, which is unremarkable and barely registers. Evidence that contradicts it arrives as a failure, which is vivid, memorable and retold.

That is the availability heuristic doing its work, and it means a reputation is a stock you can only add to in small increments and can draw down in one afternoon.

## Where practitioners get it wrong

**They run a reputation problem as a brand project.** The symptom is a company losing late-stage deals that commissions a rebrand. New identity, same loss rate, because the buyer was never confused about who they were.

**They treat reputation as communications.** Reputation follows from what a company does, mostly from how it behaves when something goes wrong. The communications function can report it and can avoid making it worse. It cannot manufacture it.

**They measure brand and assume reputation.** Awareness trackers tell you nothing about whether people trust you. Those are different questions and they need different instruments.

## What to do with it

1. Establish which one is failing before spending. If you are not on shortlists, that is brand. If you are on shortlists and losing late, that is reputation. 2. Ask lost prospects what they were worried about. Not why they chose the other supplier, what they were worried about. Different question, better answer. 3. Measure them separately. Recognition and recall on one side, trust and perceived risk on the other. 4. Put your reputation work where your failures are handled, not where your messaging is written. 5. Accept the timescale. A reputation moves over years and will not respond to a quarter of effort.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

This distinction decides where you should personally spend time, and it is usually settled by whoever asks you for budget first.

Your brand can be delegated. Someone else can own the identity, the website and the campaign, and you can review it.

Your reputation cannot be delegated, because it is produced by what the company actually does: how you price, how you behave when a project slips, whether you tell a client something they do not want to hear. Those are your decisions and your standards, and no agency can install them.

So the practical division is this. If the problem is that not enough people know you exist, that is a budget question and you can hand it over. If the problem is that people who know you are choosing somebody else, that is an operating question and it is yours.

The diagnostic question I would ask first: when a project of ours goes badly, what does the client experience, and who decides that? If nobody can answer cleanly, the reputation work starts there rather than in marketing.

Sources:

1. Fombrun, C. J. (1996). Reputation: Realizing Value from the Corporate Image. Harvard Business School Press.
2. Sharp, B. (2010). How Brands Grow: What Marketers Don't Know. Oxford University Press.

### The Edelman Trust Barometer

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/the-edelman-trust-barometer/
Date: 2026-09-12. Read: 4 min.

An annual survey of trust in four institutions, business, government, media and non-governmental organisations, published by the communications firm Edelman every year since 2001. It is the most widely cited public measure of institutional trust, and it is worth understanding both what it shows and what it is.

## What it measures

Respondents across roughly 28 countries are asked how much they trust each of the four institutions to do what is right. Results are reported as a trust index, split by country, and by what Edelman calls the informed public against the mass population.

The split is one of the more useful features. The gap between what better-educated, higher-income, media-consuming respondents believe and what everybody else believes has been one of the more durable findings in the series.

## The finding that matters for business

Across the series, business has generally scored as the most trusted of the four institutions, and in recent years it has often been the only one scoring as trusted at all. Employers specifically score higher than business in general: people trust the company they work for more than they trust companies.

That has a commercial consequence worth sitting with. If business is the institution people still extend trust to, then a company's conduct carries more weight than it used to, and the expectation attached to it is higher. Edelman's own framing has moved over the years from measuring trust toward arguing that business is now expected to act where government has not.

Treat that framing with the appropriate caution. See below.

## How to read it honestly

Three things to hold.

**It is published by a communications firm.** Edelman sells communications advisory, and the Barometer is both a genuine research instrument and the largest piece of marketing that firm produces. The data collection is serious. The interpretation layered on top is written by a company that benefits if executives conclude they need help with trust.

That does not make it wrong. It makes it a source with an interest, and you should read the charts rather than the conclusions.

**It measures stated trust, not behaviour.** What people say about trusting institutions in a survey and what they do when buying are different things, and the gap between attitude and behaviour is one of the most reliable findings in social psychology. A rising trust score does not mean anybody bought anything.

**Year-on-year comparisons are the valuable part.** A single year's number for a single country tells you very little. The direction over a decade is where the instrument earns its keep.

## Why it is in a marketing reference

Because it gets quoted constantly, usually second hand, usually as a single dramatic percentage with no year, no country and no question wording attached.

If you are going to cite it, cite the year and the market. The Barometer is a real, long-running, publicly available dataset. The version of it that circulates in slide decks is not.

## What to do with it

1. Read the actual report for your market rather than the global headline. The country-level variation is large. 2. Cite year and country every time. A Barometer figure without both is unusable. 3. Use the direction, not the level. A single year's score is noise. 4. Treat Edelman's interpretive framing separately from Edelman's data. 5. Do not substitute it for research on your own buyers. It measures trust in institutions in general, not trust in you.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The Barometer is useful to you mainly as a corrective to a particular kind of argument.

When someone proposes a trust campaign, the Barometer is usually the slide that justifies it. A big number about declining trust, no year attached, followed by a proposal. The honest reading of the data points the other way: business is the institution that has held trust best, and employers are trusted more than business in general, which suggests trust is produced by proximity and conduct rather than by campaigns.

So the question to ask is not how do we improve trust. It is where does a buyer of ours encounter evidence of how we behave, and is that evidence good.

For most B2B companies the honest answer is that the strongest trust signal they have is a reference call with an existing client, and nobody owns it, nobody prepares it, and nobody knows what gets said on it.

Sources:

1. Edelman Trust Barometer, published annually since 2001. Methodology, sample sizes and country coverage vary by year and are documented in each annual report. Cite the specific year and market.

### 1982. The Tylenol case

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/the-tylenol-case-1982/
Date: 2026-09-10. Read: 5 min.

In the autumn of 1982, seven people in the Chicago area died after taking Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules that had been laced with potassium cyanide. Johnson & Johnson pulled the product nationally, warned the public not to take it, and reintroduced it in tamper-evident packaging. It remains the reference case in crisis communications, and it is routinely misread.

## What happened

The deaths occurred over a short period and were linked to capsules bought from several different shops. The contamination had happened after the product left the company, which is to say Johnson & Johnson had not caused it and could not have prevented it through any manufacturing control.

The company nonetheless withdrew the product from the entire United States market, not from Chicago, and told consumers publicly not to take Tylenol until it was resolved. The withdrawal was enormous and the cost was substantial.

Tylenol returned to the market in new packaging with a tamper-evident seal, a format that became standard across the industry and was subsequently reinforced by federal regulation.

The person responsible was never identified. The case is open.

## Why it became the reference case

Because the company acted against its own immediate commercial interest, visibly, before it was required to.

The decision that gets taught is the national recall. The narrow commercial logic pointed to a Chicago recall: the problem was geographically contained, the company was not at fault, and a national withdrawal destroyed an enormous amount of inventory and revenue. They did it anyway.

That is the whole lesson, and it is a lesson about decision rights and standing commitments rather than about communications. The company had a credo, written decades earlier, that put patients and users first and shareholders last in order. Whether that document caused the decision or merely described a culture that would have made it anyway is not something the record settles.

## What people get wrong about it

**They read it as a public relations success.** It was an operating decision with a communications consequence. The withdrawal was the act. The press conferences reported it. Reversing that order is how companies end up believing a crisis is a messaging problem.

**They assume the recovery was immediate.** Market share fell sharply and recovery took time and substantial investment, including the packaging redesign, a coupon programme and heavy advertising. The story as usually told compresses a long and expensive year into a paragraph.

**They treat it as a template.** The circumstances were unusual in a way that matters: the company was not at fault. Most corporate crises are the opposite, and the hardest part is acknowledging fault rather than demonstrating care about someone else's. A playbook drawn from Tylenol will not survive contact with a crisis you caused.

**They forget the second one.** There was a further tampering incident in 1986, after which the company stopped selling capsules altogether and moved to caplets. The second decision is arguably the more instructive, because by then the cost was known and they did it again.

## What transfers

Three things, and only three.

The decision has to be made before the crisis, in the form of a standing rule about what you will not trade away. Decided in the moment, under cost pressure, almost nobody chooses the expensive option.

Speed matters more than completeness. They acted while facts were still unknown, which is the opposite of most legal advice.

And the response has to cost you something visible, or it does not register as sincere. An action that is free reads as public relations, because it is.

## What to do with it

1. Write down now, before anything happens, the one or two things you will not trade for revenue. Specific, not values language. 2. Decide who can order a withdrawal or a stop, and at what cost ceiling, without convening anybody. If that person does not exist, you do not have a crisis plan. 3. Separate the operating decision from the communications about it, in your own planning. Confusing them is the standard failure. 4. Assume you will be at fault. Build the plan for that case, because Tylenol's case is the rare one. 5. Budget for a slow recovery. Share returned; it did not spring back.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The reason this case is taught to executives rather than to communications teams is that the decision in it was not available to a communications team.

Somebody had to authorise destroying an enormous quantity of saleable product, quickly, on incomplete information, for a problem the company had not caused. No head of communications can make that call, and by the time it reaches a committee the moment has passed.

So the question this case puts to you is narrow and uncomfortable. If something goes seriously wrong on a Friday, who in your company can stop the thing happening, at what cost, without asking anyone? If the answer is nobody, then your crisis plan is a document about messaging and it will not help you.

The second question is what your standing commitments actually are, as opposed to what your values page says. Tylenol's credo was decades old and ranked shareholders last. That ranking was written down before it was expensive.

Sources:

1. Contemporaneous reporting and Johnson & Johnson's own published account of the 1982 and 1986 incidents. Specific figures for market share loss and recall cost vary considerably between retellings and should be taken from a primary source rather than from a case-study summary.

### Trust architecture

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/trust-architecture/
Date: 2026-09-08. Read: 4 min.

Trust architecture is Brave New's name for the deliberate arrangement of evidence a buyer encounters before they are willing to commit. It is our term, not an established concept in the literature, and this entry says so plainly because a reference work that passes off its own vocabulary as received wisdom is not a reference work.

## The problem it names

In categories where the cost of being wrong is high, consultancy, healthcare, capital, industrial supply, buyers are not primarily evaluating quality. They cannot. They lack the expertise to assess the work before it is done, which is the reason they are buying it.

So they evaluate proxies. How the firm behaves in the sales process, what other people say, whether the published material demonstrates thinking or asserts it, whether anyone will put a name to a claim.

This is not irrationality. Economists have studied it for fifty years. George Akerlof's 1970 paper on markets with asymmetric information showed what happens when buyers cannot distinguish quality before purchase: they discount everything, and good sellers are driven toward the average [1]. Michael Spence showed the counter-move, which is signalling: a seller demonstrates quality by doing something that would be too costly to fake [2].

Trust architecture is the practical version of Spence's point. The question is not what do we claim, it is what have we done that would be expensive for an incompetent firm to copy.

## The distinction that does the work

A **claim** is cheap. Anyone can write that they are rigorous.

A **signal** is costly to fake. Publishing the method so a competitor can check it. Stating what you got wrong. Showing a worked example with numbers in it. Naming the conditions under which your approach fails.

Most marketing in credibility-dependent categories is entirely claims, which is why it does not work and why everyone in those categories sounds identical. If every firm asserts rigour, the assertion carries no information.

## The four layers

This is our framework rather than a finding, and it is useful mainly as a checklist.

**What you publish.** Does it demonstrate thinking or assert competence. A reader should be able to disagree with something specific.

**What you admit.** A case study with no scar in it reads as an advertisement and gets priced as one. The willingness to document a limitation is itself the signal, because a weak firm cannot afford it.

**What others say.** Independent corroboration, which you do not control and which therefore carries more weight than anything you publish.

**What happens on contact.** How quickly you answer, whether the proposal reflects what was discussed, whether you tell them something inconvenient. This is the layer that most often contradicts the other three.

## Where it goes wrong

**Firms build layer one and stop.** A content programme that asserts expertise, no admissions, no independent corroboration, and a sales process that contradicts the published voice.

**They treat admission as risk.** It is the cheapest signal available and the most under-used, because it feels like weakness in the room where it is approved.

**The layers contradict each other.** Published material about partnership, proposals written in boilerplate. Buyers notice the contradiction and resolve it in favour of the behaviour, not the publishing.

## What to do with it

1. Audit your last five pieces of published material for one falsifiable statement each. If none contains anything a reasonable person could dispute, you are producing claims. 2. Put a documented limitation in every case study. Not a humblebrag, a real constraint and what it cost. 3. Count your independent sources. If every statement about your competence originates with you, layer three does not exist. 4. Mystery-shop your own enquiry process. The gap between layers one and four is usually the whole problem. 5. Ask of every planned asset: would this be expensive for a firm that could not do the work to produce? If not, it is a claim.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The one question worth taking from this: what do we publish that a competitor who cannot do this work would find expensive to copy?

For most firms in most professional categories the honest answer is nothing. The website, the credentials, the client logos and the language about partnership are all available to anybody, at no cost, regardless of whether they are any good. Which is precisely why buyers discount them.

The things that are expensive to fake are the ones firms avoid: publishing a method in enough detail to be checked, documenting a project that went wrong and what it cost, putting a number on a result that could be audited, saying plainly which clients you are not right for.

Each of those feels like giving something away or exposing a flaw. That feeling is the point. A signal only works because it costs something, and if it is comfortable to publish it is probably carrying no information.

The cheapest place to start is the last one. Write down who you are not for.

Sources:

1. Akerlof, G. A. (1970). The Market for Lemons: Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 84(3), 488 to 500.
2. Spence, M. (1973). Job Market Signaling. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 87(3), 355 to 374.

### Reputation risk

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/reputation-risk/
Date: 2026-09-06. Read: 4 min.

Reputation risk is the exposure a company carries from the gap between what people expect of it and what it actually does. It is not the risk of bad publicity. It is the risk that an existing gap gets discovered, which is a different thing and is managed differently.

## The definition that makes it useful

Most definitions treat reputation risk as the chance of a damaging event. That framing leads straight to crisis planning, which is the wrong instrument for most of the exposure a company carries.

Robert Eccles, Scott Newquist and Roland Schatz put the sharper version in Harvard Business Review in 2007: reputational risk arises from the gap between reputation and reality [1]. If your reputation is better than your performance, you are carrying exposure regardless of whether anything has gone wrong yet. The event does not create the risk. It reveals it.

That reframing changes what you do about it. You cannot plan your way out of a gap. You can only close it, or lower what people expect.

## The three sources

Following the same framing, exposure comes from three places.

**The reputation-reality gap.** You are believed to be better at something than you are. Every quarter that passes without discovery increases the size of the eventual correction, because the gap keeps being reinforced by your own marketing.

**Changing expectations.** The gap can open without you moving at all, because what counts as acceptable shifts. Practices that were standard become indefensible. Companies are poor at noticing this, because the change is gradual and the internal consensus moves with the industry rather than with the public.

**Weak internal coordination.** One part of the company makes a promise another part cannot keep. Sales commits to a timeline operations has not agreed. This is the most common and the least dramatic, and it produces a slow accumulation of small disappointments rather than a single event.

## Why marketing makes it worse

This is the part that belongs in a marketing reference rather than a risk one.

Marketing's job is to raise expectation. That is the function. Which means effective marketing, done on top of an unclosed gap, is actively increasing reputation risk. The better the campaign, the larger the eventual correction.

Nobody is incentivised to notice. Marketing is measured on awareness and pipeline, operations on delivery, and the distance between the two belongs to neither of them, which is why it can widen for years inside a company where every individual function is hitting its numbers and no one is doing anything wrong.

## What to do with it

1. Write down the three things buyers believe about you that are most flattering. Then establish, with evidence, whether each is true. That exercise is the whole discipline. 2. Where a belief is not supported, decide explicitly: close the gap, or stop promoting the claim. Doing neither is the default and is the exposure. 3. Check whether sales is promising anything delivery has not agreed to. Read five recent proposals against five recent project retrospectives. 4. Review what has become unacceptable in your category in the last three years, and ask whether you have moved. 5. Treat a rising marketing spend as a rising risk position unless delivery capability has moved with it.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The uncomfortable implication of this entry is that your marketing may be the largest single contributor to your reputation risk, and it will never appear that way on any report.

Every campaign that works raises what buyers expect. If delivery has not moved at the same rate, you have widened the gap and funded the widening. The company feels successful throughout, because pipeline is up and nobody has complained yet.

The test is simple and most firms never run it. Take the three strongest claims in your current marketing.
