For each, ask the person responsible for delivery whether it is true for every client, most clients, or the best ones. If the answer is "the best ones", you are marketing an exception as the standard, and the correction arrives eventually as a reference call that does not go well.

The remedy is not to market less. It is to make the claim match the floor rather than the ceiling, which costs you some conversion and removes the exposure.

One governance point. This gap sits between marketing and operations and is owned by neither, which is why it persists in well-run companies. If nobody is accountable for the distance between what is promised and what is delivered, that is a structural problem rather than a failure by anyone in particular.

Sources:

1. Eccles, R. G., Newquist, S. C. and Schatz, R. (2007). Reputation and Its Risks. Harvard Business Review, February 2007.
2. Fombrun, C. J. (1996). Reputation: Realizing Value from the Corporate Image. Harvard Business School Press.

## 06 Readings

Check our readings. The books we like, what each one argues, and one line worth keeping from each.

### How Brands Grow. Byron Sharp (2010)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/how-brands-grow-byron-sharp/
Date: 2026-09-13. Read: 4 min.

The evidence-based case that brands grow by reaching more buyers rather than by deepening loyalty among the ones they have. Built on decades of purchase panel data from the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, and the most disruptive marketing book of the last twenty years.

> Growth comes from being easy to think of and easy to buy, not from being loved by a few.

## What it argues

Three claims, in order of how much trouble each causes.

**Growth comes from penetration.** Brands get bigger by being bought occasionally by many more people, not by being bought more often by the people already buying. When a brand grows, penetration moves first and loyalty follows slightly. Not the other way round.

**Double Jeopardy.** Smaller brands are punished twice, with fewer buyers and slightly lower loyalty from them. This is a regularity across categories and decades, which means your loyalty metrics are largely a function of your size.

**Distinctiveness beats differentiation.** Buyers do not perceive much meaningful difference between brands and do not look for it. What they do is recognise. So the job is to be noticeable and easy to retrieve, not to be meaningfully distinct on an attribute.

Taken together these dismantle a great deal of received practice: loyalty programmes, narrow targeting, and most positioning work as commonly done.

## What it gets right

The evidence base is the real contribution. This is a book built on observed purchasing rather than on stated preference, across many categories and many years, and the patterns it reports replicate. That is rarer in marketing than it should be.

It is also genuinely useful at the level of decisions. Reach broadly, be consistent, build distinctive assets, make the brand easy to buy. Those are instructions a team can act on tomorrow, and most of them are cheaper than what they replace.

And it is a corrective to an industry that had drifted into treating marketing as a branch of psychology practised on small samples.

## What it is wrong about, or at least overstated on

Two things, and the book's defenders tend to concede the first and resist the second.

**Scope.** The evidence base is weighted toward frequently purchased consumer categories. The extension to considered B2B purchases, where a buying group spends months comparing a handful of suppliers, is argued more than it is demonstrated. Some of it clearly transfers, mental availability in particular. Whether "buyers do not perceive difference" survives contact with a procurement committee is a fair question that the book does not really take on.

**Tone.** The book is written as though every opposing position is simply ignorance of the data. That makes it persuasive and it makes it harder to hold alongside anything else. The useful version of Sharp sits next to Ries and Trout rather than replacing them.

## Who should read it, and who should not

**Read it** if you are responsible for a brand budget and have never seen the penetration data. It will change what you fund.

**Read it** if you are about to approve a loyalty programme.

**Do not start here** if you are a founder in a young category with a handful of customers. The laws describe established categories with many buyers, and applying them to a company with twelve clients produces confident nonsense.

## The soundbite

<p class="pull">Growth comes from being easy to think of and easy to buy, not from being loved by a few.</p>

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

This is the one book on the list I would actually ask a chief executive to read, and only the first half of it.

The reason is that it kills a specific expensive idea: that the route to growth is deepening the relationship with your best customers. That idea is intuitive, it feels prudent, and it justifies a lot of spending on people who were going to buy anyway. The data says growth comes from the opposite direction.

If you take one decision from it, make it this. Before approving anything aimed at existing customers, ask what the same money would do if aimed at people who have never bought from you. That question is not always answered in Sharp's favour, particularly in B2B with few large accounts, but it is almost never asked at all.

The caution I would attach: this is a book about large categories with many buyers. If your business has thirty clients and two of them are a third of revenue, the laws in it do not describe your situation and applying them literally will cost you.

Sources:

1. Sharp, B. (2010). How Brands Grow: What Marketers Don't Know. Oxford University Press.
2. Romaniuk, J. and Sharp, B. How Brands Grow Part 2, updated 2022, extends the work to more categories including some B2B.

### Ogilvy on Advertising. David Ogilvy (1983)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/ogilvy-on-advertising/
Date: 2026-09-11. Read: 3 min.

The working manual of the man who built Ogilvy & Mather, on headlines, layouts, research, and the difference between advertising that wins awards and advertising that sells. It is a book of craft instructions, not a theory, and it should be read as one.

> Rules learned by counting, from a man who thought the customer was intelligent and the industry was not.

## What it argues

That advertising is a trade with learnable rules, discovered by testing, and that most of the industry ignores them because the rules are unglamorous.

Ogilvy's instructions are specific to the point of being irritating. How long a headline should be. Where the caption goes. That people read captions more than body copy. That long copy outsells short copy for considered purchases. That you should put the brand name in the headline.

Each of these came from direct-response testing, where the result is measurable and arrives quickly, and Ogilvy's authority rests on having counted.

## What it gets right

The underlying posture, more than any individual rule. Ogilvy treats the customer as intelligent and busy, and he treats advertising as a job with an outcome rather than as self-expression. That is still the most useful thing in it.

The insistence on research before writing has aged perfectly. So has the observation that the people who approve advertising are not the people it is for.

And the specificity is the point. Most marketing books tell you to be relevant. This one tells you where to put the caption.

## What has aged, and how

The media environment it describes is gone. Rules calibrated for print advertisements read by people with time are not transferable wholesale to a feed.

More importantly, the evidence base is direct response. Ogilvy's rules are optimised for immediate measurable action, which Binet and Field would later show is only half the job, and the half that does not compound. A campaign built entirely to Ogilvy's rules would be very good activation and would do little for brand building over the long run.

The book also carries the attitudes of its time, and the reader should expect that rather than be surprised by it.

## Who should read it, and who should not

**Read it** if you write or approve copy. It is the best practical instruction on the craft that exists, and a morning with it improves most people's work.

**Read it** if your team confuses creativity with effectiveness.

**Do not treat it as strategy.** It is a manual for making the thing, not for deciding what thing to make. Pair it with something that covers the long term.

## The soundbite

<p class="pull">Rules learned by counting, from a man who thought the customer was intelligent and the industry was not.</p>

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

Useful to you for one reason: it is the fastest way to tell whether the work you are being shown is any good.

Ogilvy's rules give a non-specialist a set of checkable questions. Is the brand name visible. Does the headline say something specific. Is there a reason to act. Would a busy, intelligent person understand this in three seconds without anyone explaining it.

Those questions are not sufficient and they will not tell you whether the strategy is right. They will reliably catch work that is self-indulgent, and that is most of what gets presented.

The caution: do not use the book to argue for short-term, response-driven advertising only. That is what Ogilvy measured because it was measurable, and the evidence since is clear that it is half the job.

Sources:

1. Ogilvy, D. (1983). Ogilvy on Advertising. Crown.
2. Ogilvy, D. (1963). Confessions of an Advertising Man. The earlier and shorter book, and the better introduction to the man.

### Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind. Al Ries and Jack Trout (1981)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/positioning-ries-and-trout/
Date: 2026-09-09. Read: 3 min.

The book that moved the battleground from the product to the prospect's mind. Own a word, or own a place relative to the leader, before somebody else does. It began as a series of articles in Advertising Age in 1972 and has shaped how marketers talk ever since.

> You do not position a product. You position it in a mind that is already full.

## What it argues

That the mind is overloaded and defends itself by simplifying. Buyers hold a short mental ladder per category, three or four names, and a brand's position is its rung.

From that, three moves survive.

You cannot beat a leader by being a better version of them, because the rung is occupied. The first brand into a category has a structural advantage in memory that is separate from any advantage in the product. And repositioning the competition is often more achievable than repositioning yourself.

The second of these is the one that still does the most work, and it is a claim about memory rather than about quality.

## What it gets right

The central insight is correct and was genuinely new: that the contest happens in the buyer's head rather than in the product specification, and that memory is the scarce resource.

It is also the book that taught marketers to think about the competitive set from the buyer's point of view rather than from the industry's. That reframing is permanent and is now so ordinary that the book gets underrated for introducing it.

## What it is wrong about

It predates the empirical work on how little buyers actually differentiate between brands, and it assumes positioning is more controllable than the evidence supports.

The Ehrenberg-Bass position, set out most directly by Romaniuk, is that most buyers in most categories perceive little meaningful difference and do not go looking for one. If that holds in your category, then "own a word" describes an ambition rather than a mechanism, and the achievable goal is to be recognised rather than to be meaningfully distinct.

This is the sharpest live disagreement in branding and the honest answer is that both are doing work at different moments. Position for the small number actively deciding. Be recognisable for everyone else.

The book is also written with enormous confidence and no data, which is worth noticing in a field that now has some.

## Who should read it, and who should not

**Read it** for the reframing, which is short and permanent.

**Read it before Romaniuk**, not after. The argument only makes sense in that order.

**Do not** build a strategy on it alone, and be careful with it in low-interest categories, where the premise that buyers are comparing you at all may simply be false.

## The soundbite

<p class="pull">You do not position a product. You position it in a mind that is already full.</p>

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The reason this book matters to you is that it describes a constraint you cannot spend your way out of.

A buyer holds a very short list per category. Not a long one. If you are not on it, you are not in the deal, and no amount of improving the product changes that on its own.

What the book does not tell you, because it predates the evidence, is how little room there is to move. Buyers do not hold brands apart as finely as the positioning tradition assumes, and the attempt to own an abstract word, trust, innovation, partnership, is where most of this work dies. Everyone claims those.

The version I would act on: decide what you want to be the obvious choice for, make it narrow enough to be plausible, and then say it the same way for years. The narrowing is the hard part, and it is yours to do.

Sources:

1. Ries, A. and Trout, J. (1981). Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind. McGraw-Hill. First published as articles in Advertising Age, 1972.
2. Romaniuk, J. (2018). Building Distinctive Brand Assets. Oxford University Press. The strongest counter-position.

### Thinking, Fast and Slow. Daniel Kahneman (2011)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/thinking-fast-and-slow-kahneman/
Date: 2026-09-07. Read: 4 min.

Kahneman's summary of a career's work on judgement and how people decide, built around two modes of thought: a fast automatic one that runs most of the time, and a slow deliberate one that mostly arrives afterwards to justify what the first already decided.

> The fast mind decides and the slow mind writes the justification, which is why asking people why they bought is close to useless.

## What it argues

That human judgement runs on systematic shortcuts, and that the errors those shortcuts produce are predictable rather than random.

For marketing the consequences are direct. Most purchasing runs on the fast system. People do not weigh attributes, they retrieve a feeling and then construct a reason. Which means the job is usually not to win an argument but to be easy to retrieve and comfortable to choose.

The specific mechanisms matter more than the framework. Anchoring, availability, loss aversion and framing are each testable and each show up in pricing, packaging and copy.

## What it gets right

Loss aversion and anchoring have held up well and are among the better evidenced findings in the social sciences. The general point that stated preference is a poor guide to behaviour is something marketing research still has not fully absorbed, forty years on.

The book is also unusually honest about uncertainty for a popular science title, and Kahneman was careful to present System 1 and System 2 as a useful fiction rather than as two places in the brain.

## What is wrong with it, and this is the part that matters

Part of this book did not survive replication, and Kahneman said so himself.

The chapter on social priming, the work suggesting that subtle cues like words about ageing change subsequent behaviour, was built on studies that have largely failed to replicate. In 2017 Kahneman publicly acknowledged that he had placed too much faith in underpowered studies and that readers should not believe that chapter as written.

That is an extraordinary thing for an author to say and it is to his enormous credit. It is also routinely omitted when marketers cite the book, which is how priming claims continue to circulate in the trade years after the evidence collapsed.

So: cite loss aversion, anchoring and availability with confidence. Treat the priming material as superseded. And be suspicious of anybody who cites this book without knowing the difference.

## Who should read it, and who should not

**Read it** if you set prices or write offers. The chapters on anchoring, framing and loss aversion will pay for themselves.

**Read it critically.** This is the book in the trade most often quoted by people who have not read it.

**Do not** use it to justify manipulation dressed as insight. The mechanisms work regardless of whether what you are selling is good, which is an argument for care rather than for enthusiasm.

## The soundbite

<p class="pull">The fast mind decides and the slow mind writes the justification, which is why asking people why they bought is close to useless.</p>

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

Two things from this book are worth your attention and the rest is interesting rather than actionable.

**Stated preference is a poor guide to behaviour.** If a decision in your company rests on what customers said in a survey or a focus group, it rests on something weaker than it appears. What people do and what they report doing diverge systematically, not randomly. Prefer observed behaviour wherever you can get it.

**Framing changes the answer.** The same offer presented as a gain and as an avoided loss produces different responses. That applies to your pricing, your renewal conversations and your proposals, and it is nearly free to test.

The warning I would attach is about how this book gets used internally. It has become the standard citation for any claim that buyers are irrational, usually to justify a decision somebody wanted to make anyway. Kahneman himself retracted confidence in one of its chapters. Anyone quoting it as settled science on every point has not read it closely.

Sources:

1. Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, Fast and Slow. Farrar, Straus and Giroux.
2. Kahneman, D. and Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk. Econometrica, 47(2), 263 to 291.
3. On the priming chapter, see Kahneman's own public statement of 2017.

### The Long and the Short of It. Les Binet and Peter Field (2013)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/the-long-and-the-short-of-it-binet-field/
Date: 2026-09-05. Read: 3 min.

The IPA study that separated brand building from sales activation, showed they work on different timescales through different mechanisms, and put a number on the split between them. The most quoted finding in modern marketing effectiveness, and the most misquoted.

> One half of marketing produces a spike you can see and the other produces a slope you cannot, and the measurement system only rewards the spike.

## What it argues

That marketing does two different jobs which are routinely treated as one.

**Activation** produces a quick sales response that fades. It works on people already in market and its effects are visible inside a quarter.

**Brand building** works slowly, on people who are not currently buying, and compounds. Its effects are invisible in the short term, which is why it gets cut.

Campaigns doing both outperformed campaigns doing either alone, and the study reported an approximate optimal split of around 60 per cent brand building to 40 per cent activation in the consumer cases, with a different balance in business-to-business.

## What it gets right

The evidence base, which is the IPA Effectiveness Databank, roughly a thousand cases of commercially reported campaign results. That is a larger and more commercially grounded dataset than almost anything else in the field.

More importantly it explains a specific organisational failure. Activation looks accountable and brand building does not, so measurement systems reward the half that fades. The book gives a finance-literate argument for the half that compounds, which is why it changed budgets when earlier arguments for brand had not.

## What to be careful about

**The 60/40 is an average, not a prescription.** It varies by category, by brand size and by whether you are growing or defending. Applying it to your own business without checking is exactly the kind of unexamined rule-following the book argues against.

**The databank selects on success.** Cases enter because an agency submitted them to an effectiveness award. Failures are underrepresented. That does not invalidate the direction of the findings and it should temper confidence in the precision of the coefficients.

**It measured paid media in an era when that was most of the voice.** The framework still holds. Computing share of voice honestly is harder now.

## Who should read it, and who should not

**Read it** if you are arguing for brand budget with a finance function. It is the most useful document in existence for that conversation.

**Read it** if your marketing is entirely performance-driven and the returns have been flattening.

**Do not** quote the 60/40 without reading the qualifications around it, which is how most people encounter it.

## The soundbite

<p class="pull">One half of marketing produces a spike you can see and the other produces a slope you cannot, and the measurement system only rewards the spike.</p>

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

This is the book that explains why your marketing reporting is structurally misleading, and it is not misleading because anybody is being dishonest.

Activation effects show up fast and attribute cleanly. Brand effects show up slowly, through people who never clicked anything, at a moment nobody observes. So any dashboard built on attribution will systematically overstate the half that fades and understate the half that compounds. Then the budget follows the dashboard.

The practical consequence: when you cut marketing in a difficult quarter, the numbers will appear to vindicate you for several quarters. The cost arrives later, as a slow decline in how readily buyers think of you, and by then it is attributed to the market.

What I would ask for is not the 60/40 split, which is an average from other people's businesses. It is a single page showing what proportion of your spend is aimed at people ready to buy now, and what proportion at people who will be ready later. Most companies have never produced that page and are surprised by the answer.

Sources:

1. Binet, L. and Field, P. (2013). The Long and the Short of It: Balancing Short and Long-Term Marketing Strategies. Institute of Practitioners in Advertising.
2. Binet, L. and Field, P. (2007). Marketing in the Era of Accountability. IPA.
3. Work with the LinkedIn B2B Institute, 2019, covers the business-to-business variant of the split.

### Alchemy. Rory Sutherland (2019)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/alchemy-rory-sutherland/
Date: 2026-09-03. Read: 4 min.

An argument for the value of ideas that do not make logical sense but work anyway. Sutherland, vice chairman of Ogilvy UK, makes the case that the search for rational, measurable, defensible marketing has squeezed out the irrational solutions that often deliver the largest returns.

> Organisations choose the defensible option over the effective one, because nobody is ever fired for being reasonable.

## What it argues

That human behaviour is not logical, so solutions derived purely from logic will systematically miss the ones that work.

His central example is the Eurostar journey time. Engineers proposed spending an enormous sum to make the trip faster. Sutherland's point is that a fraction of that, spent on making the journey more pleasant, would have produced more satisfaction per pound. The logical solution was to reduce the number. The psychological solution was to change how the number felt.

From that: the opposite of a good idea can also be a good idea, psychological solutions are usually cheaper than technical ones, and the reason they are not chosen is that nobody gets promoted for proposing something that sounds silly.

## What it gets right

The institutional critique is sharp and correct. Organisations select for defensible decisions, not effective ones, because a decision-maker is judged on whether the reasoning was reasonable rather than on whether the outcome was good. That produces a systematic bias toward the boring option, and Sutherland names the mechanism precisely.

He is also right that cost-effectiveness and logic are not the same thing, and that the cheapest lever in most businesses is psychological rather than operational.

And he is extremely good company on the page, which matters more than it should for whether a book changes anything.

## What is wrong with it

It is unfalsifiable as presented, and that is a real problem in a reference section that otherwise insists on evidence.

The argument that illogical things sometimes work cannot be tested, because every success confirms it and every failure is explained as the wrong illogical thing. There is no version of the world the thesis would rule out.

The examples are also selected after the fact. We hear about the irrational ideas that worked. The ones that did not are not in the book, and there are necessarily many more of them.

Read alongside Sharp, the two are close to incompatible. Sharp says the answers are in the data and the industry's problem is ignoring it. Sutherland says the answers are not in the data and the industry's problem is worshipping it. They cannot both be the whole picture, and a reader should notice the conflict rather than enjoy both.

## Who should read it, and who should not

**Read it** if your organisation kills every interesting idea at the business case stage.

**Do not read it first.** Without a grounding in what is evidenced, it functions as permission to do whatever you already wanted and call it alchemy.

**Do not quote it to a finance director.** It will not land, and it should not.

## The soundbite

<p class="pull">Organisations choose the defensible option over the effective one, because nobody is ever fired for being reasonable.</p>

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The useful part of this book for you is not the marketing advice. It is the observation about how your company makes decisions.

If every proposal that reaches you arrives with a business case, and every business case rests on a projection, then you are selecting for proposals that are easy to justify rather than proposals that are likely to work. Those are different populations, and the gap between them is where the cheap wins sit.

The practical move is small. Keep a deliberate allowance for a few things a year that cannot be justified in advance, with a real budget and a short deadline, and judge them on what happened rather than on whether the reasoning was sound. Most firms do this informally for things the chief executive personally likes, which is the worst version of the same idea.

The caution: this book is the most quotable on the list and the least falsifiable. It is a corrective to over-measurement, not a licence to stop measuring, and in a company that already runs on instinct it will do harm.

Sources:

1. Sutherland, R. (2019). Alchemy: The Dark Art and Curious Science of Creating Magic in Brands, Business and Life. WH Allen.

### Influence. Robert Cialdini (1984)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/influence-cialdini/
Date: 2026-09-01. Read: 4 min.

The book that catalogued the mechanisms of persuasion into six principles, built on three years of fieldwork inside sales training, fundraising and advertising operations. It is the most useful book on this list and the most misused.

> Six mechanisms that work, written partly so you could tell when they were being used on you, and now mostly used on you.

## What it argues

That compliance professionals, the people whose living depends on getting others to say yes, have converged on a small set of techniques that work because they exploit shortcuts people rely on to decide quickly.

The six, in Cialdini's original formulation: reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, liking, authority and scarcity. A seventh, unity, was added in later work.

The method is what makes it credible. Cialdini spent three years working inside the organisations that use these techniques, which is participant observation rather than laboratory work, and the principles were then tested experimentally.

## What it gets right

The principles are real, they are supported by experimental evidence, and several have replicated well. Social proof and authority in particular are about as solid as findings in social psychology get.

The framing is also honest in a way the imitators are not. Cialdini wrote the book partly as a defence manual, so that ordinary people could recognise when these techniques were being used on them. That intent is visible throughout and it is the reason the book has aged better than the genre it created.

## What goes wrong with it

Almost everything downstream.

This is the most misapplied book in marketing. The principles get deployed as tactics without the conditions that make them work, which produces the fake countdown timer, the invented scarcity, the "17 people are viewing this" notice. Cialdini has been consistently clear that manufactured social proof and false scarcity are both unethical and, over time, ineffective, because they train people to discount the signal.

There is a deeper tension worth naming. Scarcity, one of the six, is in direct conflict with the availability argument in Sharp: make it harder to get versus make it as easy to buy as possible. Both have evidence behind them. The resolution is that they operate at different moments and in different categories, and anyone applying scarcity in a category where customers already experience you as unreliable is adding to a problem rather than creating desire.

Some of the specific studies in the original have also been affected by the wider replication problems in social psychology. The core principles hold; the individual anecdotes should not be quoted as though each were separately bulletproof.

## Who should read it, and who should not

**Read it** to recognise what is being done to you. That was the author's stated purpose and it remains the best reason.

**Read it** if you write offers or sales copy, with the ethical sections included rather than skipped.

**Do not** hand it to a sales team as a tactics manual. That is how you end up with fake urgency and a reputation problem.

## The soundbite

<p class="pull">Six mechanisms that work, written partly so you could tell when they were being used on you, and now mostly used on you.</p>

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

There is a governance question in this book and it is worth taking seriously.

The six principles work. They work whether or not what you are selling is good, which means they are available to your team as a way of hitting a number without improving anything. The techniques that cross the line, invented scarcity, manufactured social proof, false deadlines, are cheap, effective in the short run, and almost never explicitly authorised. They appear because somebody is under pressure.

So the useful move is to decide, in advance and in writing, which of these you will not use. Specifically: no countdown that resets, no scarcity claim that is not true, no review or testimonial that was not freely given, no "recommended by" that was paid for without disclosure.

That list costs you a little conversion. It also means that when a buyer checks one of your claims, and in a considered purchase somebody always does, the claim holds. That is worth more than the conversion, and it is the kind of decision that only gets made at your level before it is needed.

Sources:

1. Cialdini, R. B. (1984). Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion. First edition; revised and expanded in later editions, including Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion, New and Expanded, 2021, which adds unity as a seventh principle.
2. Cialdini, R. B. (2016). Pre-Suasion. On the moment before the message, and arguably the more original book.

## 07 Research

Original studies from the Hive: how AI engines answer marketing questions, what people type into a search box, and what that means for a brand. Every number comes from a named tool on a stated date.

### How AI engines answer marketing questions: a citation study

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/research/how-ai-engines-answer-marketing-questions/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 5 min.

We asked a live AI engine eight marketing questions and checked every source it named. It performed a live search for two of them. Of the sources it listed for the rest, 21 did not exist. This is our own test, run on one engine on one day, and the method and its limits are below.

<div class="method">

## Method

**Date.** 14 September 2026. **Engine.** Gemini, gemini-3-flash-preview, with Google Search grounding enabled. **Sample.** One answer per question. Eight questions. US English. **Check.** Every URL the model named was requested and its HTTP status recorded. Working files: the listed sources, the status check per URL, the resolved grounding redirects, and the grounded page titles. **Not sampled.** ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Mode.

That is a small sample and we are not going to pretend otherwise. One engine, one country, one day, one answer per prompt. Read it as a first cut that produced a clear enough signal to be worth reporting, not as a measurement of AI search in general.

</div>

## Finding 1. The engine usually did not look anything up

Live retrieval fired for two of the eight questions.

The two were "is there a marketing encyclopedia or wiki" and "what is a [retrievable brand](/ai-marketing/what-is-a-retrievable-brand/)". Both are questions about current, contested, fast-moving topics.

The six where it did not search were basic principles of marketing, the history of marketing and advertising, neuromarketing studies, building a B2B brand for AI search, movies about marketing, and songs about advertising. Those were answered from the model's training data, with no search performed.

The split is not random. Evergreen knowledge gets answered from memory. Fresh and contested topics get looked up.

## Finding 2. When it does not look, it invents the sources

This is the part that should change how people read AI citation reports.

Where retrieval did not fire, the engine still produced a list of sources. Those lists looked entirely ordinary: real domains, plausible paths, titles that fit the claim.

We checked all of them. Across the questions where sources were listed rather than grounded, 21 URLs returned 404 or failed to resolve, 17 existed, and 14 blocked automated checking so could not be confirmed either way.

Roughly two in five of the checkable sources were not real.

The worst case was songs about advertising and consumerism: of eight sources listed, one existed and six did not. No page anywhere owns that answer, so the model filled the gap with plausible-looking addresses.

By contrast, the question where retrieval did fire properly, "what is a retrievable brand", returned 16 grounded citations and all 16 existed.

So the pattern is clean. Grounded answers cite real pages. Ungrounded answers produce a bibliography that looks like research and is not.

## Finding 3. Who owns the answers that are grounded

For "what is a retrievable brand", the 16 real citations broke down as two platform vendors, two trade publications, two companies using the term as a product name, seven small agency or consultant blogs, and one Medium post.

Not a single established marketing institution. The term is being defined in public by whoever wrote a definition-first explainer with question headings and a date on it.

Every cited page shared that shape.

## What this means if you are trying to be cited

**Establish whether the engine retrieves for your category before spending anything.** If it answers from memory, page-level work does not reach it, and the lever is third party mention over a much longer timescale.

**Check citation reports before believing them.** If a tool shows your brand cited in AI answers, click the URLs. Some proportion of them may not exist.

**Definition-first pages with question headings and visible dates are what got cited** in the one grounded answer we could analyse in depth. That is a sample of one answer and should be treated as a hypothesis rather than a rule.

## Limitations, stated plainly

One engine. One day. One sample per question. No statistical claim is being made and none should be read in. Engines change retrieval behaviour without announcing it, and this test will need repeating before any of it can be called a trend.

We publish it because the direction was strong enough to be useful and because nobody else seems to be checking whether the citations are real.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

One instruction from this, and it costs nothing.

If anyone shows you a dashboard reporting that your brand is being cited in AI answers, ask them to open three of the citations in front of you. In our test roughly two in five of the checkable sources did not exist.

A citation report is not evidence until somebody has clicked the links. That is not a criticism of any particular tool, it is a property of how these systems produce source lists when they have not actually searched.

The second question worth asking: does the engine look anything up when our buyers ask their questions, or does it answer from memory? If it answers from memory, then any programme of website changes is addressed to a mechanism that is not running, and the honest route is slower and mostly involves other people writing about you.

### How the AI search vocabulary moved in a year

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/research/how-the-ai-search-vocabulary-moved/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 4 min.

Three terms compete to name the same worry: that buyers are asking an AI assistant instead of a search engine. We tracked all three in US search volume across a year. AI SEO is the largest, generative engine optimization peaked early and fell back, and answer engine optimization climbed from almost nothing to a real number. Our own data, fetched 14 September 2026.

<div class="method">

## Method

**Source.** Ubersuggest, US locale, English. Monthly search volume. **Fetched.** 14 September 2026. **Terms.** [AI SEO](/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-seo/), [AI marketing](/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-marketing/), [generative engine optimization](/ai-marketing/what-is-generative-engine-optimization/), [answer engine optimization](/ai-marketing/what-is-answer-engine-optimization/), and their close variants. **Limit.** Ubersuggest hit its daily cap of 150 keyword reports during the run. Eight planned keywords returned HTTP 403 and are recorded as no data rather than as zero.

Search volume estimates are modelled, not measured. Treat the relative sizes and the direction of travel as the signal, and the absolute numbers as approximate.

</div>

## The standing position

| Term | US monthly volume | Difficulty | CPC | |---|---|---|---| | AI SEO | 8,100 | 54 | $41.79 | | AI marketing | 5,400 | 61 | $32.29 | | Generative engine optimization | 4,400 | 74 | $28.56 | | AI marketing tools | 4,400 | 47 | $34.55 | | Answer engine optimization | 2,400 | 56 | $32.53 | | Generative engine optimization (GEO) | 1,600 | 69 | $29.66 |

The cost per click is the number that tells you this is a real market rather than a conversation. AI SEO at nearly $42 a click is expensive, and nobody bids that for a term buyers are not using.

## The movement, which matters more than the level

Two trajectories in opposite directions.

**Answer engine optimization climbed hardest.** It went from 210 searches a month in August 2025 to 1,600 in June 2026 and 2,400 in July 2026. That is the steepest climb in the whole dataset, from a term almost nobody was using to one with real volume in under a year.

**Generative engine optimization peaked and fell back.** It reached 6,600 in August and September 2025 and has sat between 3,600 and 5,400 since.

So the term with the research paper behind it peaked early, and the term with no literature at all is the one still growing. That is a useful corrective to the assumption that vocabulary follows evidence. It mostly follows whoever is publishing.

## A note on one number we threw out

"Marketing fundamentals" returned a headline volume of 301,000, which would have made it one of the largest terms in the study.

The monthly series makes it unusable: 1,500,000 in July 2025, 1,830,000 in August 2025, 90,500 in September, 4,400 in October, then between 210 and 590 a month from November 2025 to June 2026, then 301,000 in July 2026.

A term does not behave like that. It is a data artefact, the steady-state months put it in the thin band, and we excluded it. We mention it because this is exactly the kind of number that ends up in a slide as evidence of enormous demand.

## What to take from it

1. The vocabulary has not settled, so do not build a brand on one of these terms as though it were permanent. 2. AI SEO is the term with the most demand and the highest commercial intent. If you are writing to be found, it is the one that pays. 3. AEO is the growth term. If the climb continues, the position is cheaper to take now than later. 4. Always look at the monthly series, never the headline figure. One of the six terms we checked was an artefact.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The decision this bears on is whether to name something in your business after one of these terms.

The honest read: the vocabulary is a year old, one of the three terms has already peaked and declined, and the one growing fastest has no research behind it. Any service line, page or job title built on one of them is a bet on which word survives.

That is an argument for describing what you do in durable language and using the current vocabulary only where buyers search for it. Name the service for the outcome. Use the term of the month in the page title where the demand is.

The second thing worth your attention is the cost per click. Over $30 a click across all of these means you are entering an auction against venture-funded software companies. Paid search is not where a services business wins this, and anyone proposing it should be made to show the maths.

### What people search for in marketing: the demand map

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/research/what-people-search-for-in-marketing/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 5 min.

We measured US monthly search volume for every topic a marketing reference site might cover. Three findings. Film titles are the largest entries by a wide margin, concept names beat author names by roughly two hundred to one, and two categories we had planned barely exist as searches. Our own data, fetched 14 September 2026.

<div class="method">

## Method

**Source.** Ubersuggest, US locale, English. Monthly search volume and SEO difficulty. **Fetched.** 14 September 2026. **Scope.** Every planned section and entry for the Hive, plus close variants. **Verdict rule, applied consistently.** Searched means 500 or more a month. Thin means 50 to 490. Dead means under 50. **Limit.** The daily cap of 150 keyword reports was reached. Eight keywords returned HTTP 403 and are recorded as no data, not as zero.

Volumes are modelled estimates. Relative size is the signal.

</div>

## Finding 1. The films are bigger than the marketing

| Entry | Keyword | US monthly volume | |---|---|---| | The Founder | the founder movie | 74,000 | | Thank You for Smoking | thank you for smoking | 22,200 | | Marketing mix | marketing mix | 14,800 | | The 4 Ps of marketing | 4 ps of marketing | 12,100 | | Market segmentation | market segmentation | 9,900 | | Positioning in marketing | positioning in marketing | 9,900 | | Loss aversion | loss aversion | 8,100 | | How to Get Ahead in Advertising | how to get ahead in advertising | 1,900 | | Movies about advertising | movies about advertising | 1,300 | | Marketing terms | marketing terms | 1,000 |

One film title carries more search volume than the entire marketing theory section combined. That does not mean we should become a film site. It means the section name "movies about advertising" at 1,300 a month is the realistic target, because competing for "the founder movie" against the studios and the film databases is not a contest we would win.

## Finding 2. Concept names beat author names, overwhelmingly

[Positioning in marketing](/principles/positioning-in-marketing/): 9,900 a month. Positioning, Ries and Trout, phrased as "positioning ries trout": 50 a month. "Positioning the battle for your mind", the actual book title: 480.

A ratio of roughly two hundred to one between the idea and the men who named it.

This is the single most actionable finding in the study and it decided how every entry on the site is titled. People search for what a thing is, not for who said it. An entry called "Positioning in marketing" gets found. An entry called "Ries and Trout" does not, however much more scholarly it feels.

The same pattern held everywhere we checked it.

## Finding 3. Two planned sections have almost no demand

**Songs.** "Songs about marketing" returns 70 a month. "Songs about advertising" returns 30, which is below our dead threshold. "Songs about consumerism" 110, "songs about capitalism" 170.

The adjacent demand is real and we are not serving it: songs about money 4,400, songs about greed 1,900.

**Neuromarketing deep cuts.** The head term "neuromarketing" is healthy at 1,900. Everything under it collapses: neuromarketing meaning 140, examples 90, career 90, techniques 40.

We are keeping both sections. It is worth being explicit about why, because the numbers say not to.

Songs exists because nobody owns the topic, because the citation study found that no page anywhere answers that question properly, and because a reference site assembled purely from search volume reads like it was built by a machine. It will not bring traffic and it is not resourced as though it will.

## What this changed

1. Every section renamed to the searched phrasing. History of marketing (210) became history of advertising (720). Movies about marketing (590) became movies about advertising (1,300). 2. Every entry titled by concept rather than by author. 3. Songs and the thinner neuromarketing entries kept, but deliberately deprioritised rather than resourced equally. 4. No section built on a term with no demand without a stated non-traffic reason for keeping it.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The transferable finding here has nothing to do with marketing reference sites.

It is that your customers search for the problem, and your company names things after the solution. Those are different vocabularies and the gap between them is usually invisible from inside, because everyone internally has learned the internal words.

The two hundred to one ratio between "positioning in marketing" and the names of the men who invented it is an extreme version of something that is true of nearly every business. Your proprietary framework name, your service line name, your product name: nobody is searching for any of them. They are searching for the thing that is wrong.

A cheap test. Take the five page titles on your website that matter most and check the monthly search volume for each exact phrase. If they are all under fifty, your site is organised around your own vocabulary rather than your buyers' questions.

That is fixable in an afternoon of retitling and it is usually the highest return hour available.

## 08 Movies about advertising

Films and series about advertising, persuasion, brands and the people who sell them. Year, director and what each one is really about.

### Thank You for Smoking (2005)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/thank-you-for-smoking/
Date: 2026-09-05. Read: 3 min.

Jason Reitman's satire follows a tobacco lobbyist who can argue any side of any question. It is a film about spin, about the gap between persuasion and truth, and about what happens to a person who is very good at the first and indifferent to the second.

## What it is

Adapted from Christopher Buckley's novel, with Aaron Eckhart as Nick Naylor, chief spokesman for a tobacco industry front organisation. He is charming, quick, entirely without conviction, and the film declines to punish him for it.

## What it gets right about the trade

**It understands that the skill is real.** Naylor is not stupid and he is not a fraud. He is genuinely excellent at argument, and the film takes that seriously rather than treating persuasion as a trick anyone could do.

**It identifies the actual move.** Naylor's technique is not to prove his side is right. It is to make his opponent's position look like an attack on freedom or on the audience's intelligence. Shifting the question rather than answering it is the most common manoeuvre in commercial communications and this film dramatises it better than any textbook.

**The conflict-of-interest machinery is accurate.** Front organisations, funded research, friendly experts. That infrastructure existed and the film is not exaggerating it.

## What it gets wrong

It is a comedy about something that killed an enormous number of people, and it is cheerful. Naylor pays essentially no price. That is a deliberate choice and it makes the satire sharper, but it also lets the audience enjoy the skill without sitting with the consequence.

It also flatters our trade slightly. Real commercial persuasion is far more boring than Naylor, and most of it is done by people with no talent for argument at all.

## The one scene worth showing a team

The ice cream scene with his son, where Naylor explains that if you argue correctly you are never wrong, and demonstrates it by refusing to defend chocolate and instead attacking the premise that one flavour must be best.

Show it, then ask the team to find the same move in your own category's marketing. It is always there.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The reason to watch this is to get better at spotting the move when it is used on you, including by your own people.

Reframing the question instead of answering it is the standard response to an uncomfortable number. You ask why the pipeline is down and receive an articulate explanation of why pipeline is the wrong metric. You ask why a campaign underperformed and are told the goal was always awareness.

Both answers may be true. Both are also exactly what you would hear if they were not. The test is whether the reframing was offered before the result or after it.

The cheap discipline: write down what the measure of success is, and what number would count as failure, before the work starts. Once that exists, the move stops working, and good people stop needing it.

### The Founder (2016)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/the-founder/
Date: 2026-09-01. Read: 3 min.

Ray Kroc turns a single hamburger stand in San Bernardino into McDonald's. The product was the brothers'. The system was theirs too. The brand, the real estate and the name became his. It is the best film ever made about what a brand actually is, and it is not a flattering answer.

## What it is

John Lee Hancock's 2016 film, with Michael Keaton as Kroc, telling the story of how a milkshake-mixer salesman encountered the McDonald brothers' restaurant, franchised it, and ended up owning the company and the name while the brothers were pushed out.

## What it gets right about the trade

**It separates the product from the brand, and shows which one captures the value.** The brothers invented the operating system: the kitchen layout, the speed, the limited menu. It was genuinely brilliant and it is why the food was good. Kroc contributed none of it. He understood what it could be called, where it could be put, and how it could be owned.

That is uncomfortable and it is accurate. Operational excellence does not automatically become market position. Somebody has to do the second job and it is a different job.

**It understands consistency as the product.** The thing Kroc was selling to franchisees and customers was sameness. Not the best hamburger, the same hamburger. That is distinctiveness and physical availability several decades before anyone wrote it down.

**The real estate insight is the actual business model**, and the film gives it the weight it deserves. The money was in owning the land under the restaurants. Most people who cite this film as a branding story miss that the branding was in service of a property play.

## What it gets wrong

It is a film, and it compresses and dramatises. The brothers are played as pure and Kroc as the predator, which makes for a better story than the record probably supports.

It also invites a reading that the brand work was theft. The more honest reading is that the brothers built something excellent and had no interest in scaling it, and Kroc did the work they would not do. The ruthlessness is real. So is the fact that without him it stays one restaurant.

## The one scene worth showing a team

Kroc explaining why the name matters. He says McDonald's sounds like America, and that his own name would never have worked.

It is thirty seconds and it is the cleanest statement of brand asset value in any film. A name that is memorable, pronounceable and carries the right associations is worth more than the recipe, and the person who recognised that is the person who ended up owning the company.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

This is the film to watch if you have built something good and cannot understand why a less competent competitor is better known.

The McDonald brothers were better operators than Kroc, by a distance. They lost anyway, because they treated the thing they had built as the whole job. Being excellent at delivery and assuming recognition follows is the most common failure mode among technically strong founders, and it is the central subject of this film.

Two questions it raises that are worth sitting with. Who in your business owns the job of making you known, as distinct from making you good? And if the answer is nobody, or a junior person reporting to someone with a different priority, that is the structural version of the brothers' mistake.

The second: what do you actually own? Kroc's answer turned out to be the land. For most service businesses the honest answer is the client relationships, and those sit with individual people who can leave.

### Art & Copy (2009)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/art-and-copy/
Date: 2026-08-28. Read: 3 min.

Doug Pray's documentary on the creative revolution in American advertising, with Lee Clow, George Lois, Mary Wells Lawrence, Hal Riney and others talking about the work that defined the trade. It is the most affectionate film on this list and the least critical.

## What it is

A feature documentary, interviews intercut with the campaigns themselves, built around the generation who moved advertising away from product claims and toward ideas.

## What it gets right about the trade

**The people are the real archive.** Hearing Mary Wells Lawrence and George Lois describe their own decisions, in their own words, is primary source material and it will not exist for much longer. That alone justifies the film.

**It shows the campaigns at length.** Not clips, the actual work. You can see why it was good rather than being told.

**It captures what changed.** The move from explaining a product to building an association is the single biggest shift in twentieth century advertising, and the film documents the people who made it without turning it into a lecture.

## What it gets wrong

It is a celebration and it does not pretend otherwise, which is fine, but it means the film has no argument and no doubt in it.

Nobody in it discusses a campaign that failed. Nobody mentions effectiveness measurement, which was developing throughout the period covered. The implicit thesis, that great creative work is self-evidently valuable, is exactly the assumption that the IPA databank was built to test, and the film predates none of that work.

So it is a good film about craft and a poor film about whether the craft worked.

## The one part worth showing a team

The Lee Clow material on the 1984 Apple commercial.

Not for the commercial, which everyone has seen, but for the account of what it took to get it approved and how close it came to being killed. That is the useful part for any team that believes the hard thing is having the idea. The hard thing is almost always getting it through the room.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

Watch it for one thing: a sense of what a strong creative idea actually looks like, so you can recognise the difference between distinctive work and work that is merely competent.

Then apply the correction the film does not provide. Every campaign in it is one that worked, selected decades later by people who made them. You are seeing survivors, which tells you nothing about the base rate.

The practical version for your own business is a question your agency will not enjoy. Of the work you have made for clients like us, what proportion hit its number? A team with evidence will tell you. A team that answers by showing you a reel is doing what this film does, and it is lovely and it is not evidence.

### The Greatest Movie Ever Sold (2011)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/the-greatest-movie-ever-sold/
Date: 2026-08-22. Read: 3 min.

Morgan Spurlock makes a documentary about product placement, funded entirely by product placement, and films himself selling the sponsorships. The premise is a gimmick and the footage of the actual sales meetings is the most honest thing ever recorded about how brand partnerships are negotiated.

## What it is

Spurlock sets out to finance the film by selling placement within it, and documents every pitch. Brands appear as sponsors of a film about the practice of sponsoring films. The formal title carries a sponsor name, which is the joke.

## What it gets right about the trade

**The meetings are real and they are the film.** We see brand managers and their agencies deciding what they will and will not be associated with, in their own words, with the camera running. Nothing else in this section gets that access.

**It demonstrates how much control sponsors expect.** The negotiations are mostly about approval rights, context and adjacency, not about money. That is accurate and it is the part most people outside the industry get wrong.

**The rejections are more informative than the acceptances.** Watching brands decline because the association is slightly wrong is a better education in brand safety than any policy document.

## What it gets wrong

The reflexive structure eats the subject. By the end it is a film about making the film, and the actual question, what placement does to audiences and whether it works, is barely examined.

There is no evidence in it. We learn a great deal about how deals are made and nothing about whether placement shifts preference, which is the only question a marketer would want answered.

It is also, unavoidably, a stunt. Spurlock's method produces access and limits depth, and this one leans further toward the stunt than his earlier work.

## The one part worth showing a team

Any of the pitch meetings, chosen at random.

Watch a brand team articulate what they are protecting. That articulation, unrehearsed and commercially real, is the closest thing to a brand strategy most companies ever produce, and it only comes out when someone asks them to approve an association.

Then ask your own team: what would we refuse, and why? Most cannot answer.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The useful exercise from this film costs an hour.

Ask your marketing lead what partnership or association your company would turn down, and why. Not in principle, specifically: which sponsorship, which co-marketing deal, which publication.

If the answer is vague, you do not have a brand position, you have a logo and a colour. The brands in this film could all answer instantly, because they had been forced to decide in advance, and the deciding is the work.

The second observation worth taking: the negotiations were about control and context, not price. When your company is the one being associated with something, the same should be true. If a partnership conversation in your business is only about cost, somebody has skipped the part that matters.

### The Century of the Self (2002)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/the-century-of-the-self/
Date: 2026-08-17. Read: 3 min.

Adam Curtis's four-part BBC documentary on how Freud's ideas about the unconscious were taken up by business and government to manage the public. The most useful thing on this list, and the only one that is really about marketing rather than about advertising people.

## What it is

Four hours, made for the BBC, tracing a line from Sigmund Freud through his nephew Edward Bernays, who applied psychoanalytic ideas to public relations in the United States, to the motivational research of the 1950s, to the self-actualisation movement, to the political consultancy of the 1990s.

The argument is that the twentieth century saw a shift from treating people as rational citizens with needs to treating them as consumers with desires, and that this was a deliberate project with named authors rather than a drift.

## What it gets right about the trade

**Bernays is the correct starting point and almost nobody in marketing has read him.** He is the direct link between a theory of the unconscious and the practice of mass persuasion, and he was explicit about what he was doing in a way that would be unpublishable now.

**It takes the techniques seriously as techniques.** The series does not treat persuasion as silly or as obviously evil. It treats it as something that works, which is far more unsettling and far more useful.

**It connects marketing to politics without being glib about it.** The same methods, the same consultants, moving between the two. That is historically accurate and it is the part of our trade's history most often left out of the telling.

## What it gets wrong, or at least overstates

Curtis builds an argument by juxtaposition. Archive footage, a flat narration, a cut to something ominous. It is enormously persuasive and it is not an argument you can check.

The thesis is also too tidy. It presents a century of messy, competing, frequently failing commercial activity as a coherent project executed by a small number of people who understood what they were doing. Most of marketing history is people guessing.

And there is an irony the series never addresses: it is itself a masterpiece of emotional persuasion through editing, making an argument about the dangers of emotional persuasion.

## The one part worth showing a team

Episode one, the Bernays material on the 1929 cigarette campaign, where he arranged for women to smoke publicly at a parade and framed it as a gesture of emancipation.

It is the clearest demonstration in any film of the difference between selling a product and attaching it to an identity. It is also a direct illustration of how much damage that technique can do when the product is harmful, which makes it a better conversation starter with a team than any case study.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

Worth four hours of your time, and not for the marketing.

The thing it will give you is a working sense of how old these techniques are and how deliberately they were built. Most executives encounter persuasion methods as new, arriving with a vendor and a deck. They are not new. The intellectual work was done in the 1920s and everything since is implementation.

That matters practically, because it changes how you evaluate a proposal. When somebody presents a behavioural technique as a breakthrough, the useful question is which of the old mechanisms this is, and whether it is being used on people in a way you would defend if it were described plainly to them.

The series is also a reasonable inoculation against your own marketing. If you watch four hours of how effectively this works on populations, you will be slightly less confident that it does not work on you.

### How to Get Ahead in Advertising (1989)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/how-to-get-ahead-in-advertising/
Date: 2026-08-11. Read: 3 min.

Bruce Robinson's film in which an advertising executive, unable to write a campaign for a spot cream, has a breakdown and grows a talking boil on his neck that argues for the industry he has come to hate. It is the only genuinely angry comedy about advertising, and it is about what the work does to the person doing it.

## What it is

Richard E. Grant as Dennis Bagley, from the director of Withnail and I. The boil develops a face and a voice, expresses everything Bagley has suppressed about selling, and eventually takes over.

## What it gets right about the trade

**The moral injury is the subject.** Not whether advertising is good or bad for society, but what it costs the individual to spend years arguing for things they do not believe. That is a real occupational hazard and this is the only film that treats it as the main event.

**The language is exact.** Bagley's monologues are a precise parody of agency speech, the rhetorical escalation, the self-importance, the way a trivial brief gets discussed as though it were a moral question. Anyone who has sat in those meetings recognises the register immediately.

**The split is the right metaphor.** The part of him that can sell anything does not go away when he rejects it. It becomes a separate voice and it is more confident than he is.

## What it gets wrong

It is a rant, and it does not distinguish between advertising that is harmful and advertising that is merely commerce. Selling a spot cream is treated with the same horror as selling a war, which weakens rather than sharpens the argument.

It is also wildly uneven in tone and the second half loses control. That is arguably the point and it is still hard to watch.

## The one part worth showing a team

Bagley's monologue about the function of advertising, delivered at speed and with total conviction.

It is a better articulation of the cynical case against the trade than anyone hostile to it has managed, and it comes from inside. Useful to show precisely because it is not a straw man.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

This one is about retention and it is not usually read that way.

The condition the film describes, being required to argue daily for things you do not believe, is a real cause of good people leaving commercial roles. It rarely appears in an exit interview, because it sounds self-indulgent and because nobody wants to say it to the person who set the brief.

The practical question for you: do the people writing your marketing believe the claims in it? If they do not, you will lose them, and before you lose them the work will get worse in a way that is hard to diagnose, because unconvinced copy is technically fine and does nothing.

The cheap test is to ask a writer to defend a claim without using the words from the brief. If they cannot, either the claim is not true or they have not been told why it is.

### The Joneses (2009)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/the-joneses/
Date: 2026-08-05. Read: 3 min.

A family moves into an affluent suburb and is admired for their taste, their possessions and their apparent ease. They are not a family. They are a unit of stealth marketers, placed to make their neighbours want what they have. The premise is better than the film, and the premise is worth an hour of anyone's attention.

## What it is

Derrick Borte's 2009 film with David Duchovny and Demi Moore as two of the four operatives, selling by being envied rather than by advertising.

## What it gets right about the trade

**Social proof as a product.** The entire operation rests on Cialdini's principle: people decide what to want by observing what people like them already have. The film dramatises it more clearly than any explanation.

**The absence of a message.** The Joneses never make a claim. They own things and are admired. That is the whole mechanism and it is precisely why it works, because there is nothing to argue with.

**It anticipates the influencer economy by several years.** Made before the model was named, it describes it exactly: paid people performing an aspirational life, with the commercial relationship concealed.

## What it gets wrong

The film loses its nerve. It sets up a sharp satire and resolves into a conventional drama about the characters' feelings, which is less interesting than the premise it abandoned.

It also treats the mechanism as exotic. By 2009 it was not, and it is now entirely ordinary and partly regulated. Disclosure rules in most markets now require exactly what the Joneses conceal, which dates the film in a useful way.

## The one part worth showing a team

The scene where a neighbour, having bought everything the Joneses have, cannot afford it and the consequence lands.

Show it when discussing influencer work, because it is the clearest statement of who carries the cost when aspiration is manufactured well. The question is not whether the technique works. It is what happens to the person it works on.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The relevant issue here is disclosure, and it is a live compliance question rather than a philosophical one.

Undisclosed paid endorsement is now regulated in most of the markets you operate in, and enforcement has been getting less forgiving. If your company pays anybody to talk about it, including employees with their own audiences, the commercial relationship has to be visible.

Two practical things. Put the disclosure requirement in the contract rather than in a briefing email, so it is enforceable. And decide who checks that it actually happened, because in most companies nobody does and the exposure sits with you rather than with the creator.

The broader point the film makes is worth keeping too. Manufactured aspiration works, and it works on people who cannot afford the thing. In a B2B context the equivalent is selling a capability to a company that does not have the maturity to use it. It closes, and it churns, and it costs you a reference.

### Mad Men (2007 to 2015)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/mad-men/
Date: 2026-07-30. Read: 3 min.

Matthew Weiner's series about a New York advertising agency in the 1960s. It is the most influential depiction of our trade ever made, it is extremely good, and it is a period drama that a surprising number of people in marketing have quietly absorbed as a documentary.

## What it is

Seven seasons on AMC, following Don Draper and the agency around him from 1960 to 1970. Created by Matthew Weiner, who came to it from The Sopranos.

## What it gets right about the trade

**The pitch is the product.** The series understands that in an agency the thing being sold in the room is not the advertisement, it is the conviction of the person presenting it. That remains true and it is still the uncomfortable centre of how this business works.

**The client relationship is the actual job.** Most of the drama concerns account management rather than creative work: who holds the relationship, and what happens when it moves. Correct, and almost never depicted anywhere else.

**The period detail on the business is careful.** The shift from founder-dominated shops to holding companies, the arrival of research, the early computing, the slow entry of women into creative roles. Weiner's team did the work.

## What it gets wrong, and this is the important part

It makes the work look like inspiration.

Draper's method is to withdraw, suffer, and return with a complete idea that silences the room. That is a dramatic necessity and it is a lie about how advertising is made. Real campaigns come from briefs, research, argument, twenty rejected routes and a compromise. Nobody closes their eyes and receives the Carousel.

This matters because the myth is load-bearing in the industry. It justifies creative teams who will not explain their reasoning, agencies that resist measurement, and a general preference for the brilliant individual over the disciplined process. Binet and Field's databank exists partly because this model of how advertising works produced so little evidence.

The series also depicts an industry that no longer exists, in which the agency held the client relationship, the media and the authority. Watching it as aspiration rather than as history is a career error.

## The one episode worth showing a team

The Carousel pitch at the end of season one.

Show it for what it does well, which is the demonstration that people buy a feeling and construct a reason afterwards. Then say plainly that the scene is fiction, that nobody works this way, and that the pitch is good because a writer spent weeks on it rather than because a man had an epiphany.

Both halves of that conversation matter.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

Useful to you as a diagnostic of your own agency relationships.

If the people presenting work to you do it the way Draper does, with a reveal, a narrative and no visible reasoning, that is a style borrowed from television and it should make you more sceptical rather than less. Good work survives being explained. A route that only persuades when performed is a route you cannot evaluate.

The question that cuts through it: what else did you consider, and why did you reject it? A team with a process answers that easily and the answer is interesting. A team selling you inspiration will treat the question as an insult.

The other thing worth noticing is how much of the series is about the account relationship rather than the work, because that part is still true. If your agency relationship depends on one person who likes you, you have a concentration risk and not a partnership.

### Putney Swope (1969)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/putney-swope/
Date: 2026-07-24. Read: 3 min.

Robert Downey Sr's satire in which the token Black executive at a New York advertising agency is accidentally elected chairman, fires almost everyone, renames the firm Truth and Soul, and refuses to take tobacco, alcohol or war toy accounts. It is the angriest film on this list and the most interesting.

## What it is

A low-budget independent film from 1969, shot largely in black and white with the commercials themselves in colour. Written and directed by Robert Downey Sr.

## What it gets right about the trade

**It is about who gets to make the work**, which is a question the industry was not asking in 1969 and took another fifty years to take seriously. That alone makes it the most prescient film here.

**The accidental election is a real mechanism.** Swope wins because every board member votes for the person they assume nobody else will vote for. Anyone who has sat on a committee recognises it immediately, and it is a sharper piece of organisational observation than anything in Mad Men.

**The commercials within the film are better than most real ones**, which is the joke and also the argument. The new agency makes work that is funnier, stranger and more memorable than the industry it replaced.

## What it gets wrong, or where it complicates itself

Swope's principles erode. He keeps the war toy account by another name, the agency becomes what it displaced, and the film ends in something close to nihilism.

Whether that is honest or cynical is a real question. It can be read as the system being unchangeable, which is a convenient conclusion for anybody inside it. It can also be read as a warning about what happens when a reform depends on one person's character rather than on a rule.

The film is also chaotic, uneven and very much of its moment. Some of it has aged badly and a viewer should expect that.

## The one part worth showing a team

The board meeting where Swope is elected.

Four minutes, and it is the best depiction of how organisations make decisions nobody intended. Show it before any committee process in your own firm and watch people get uncomfortable.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

Two things in this film are about running an organisation rather than about advertising.

The first is the election. Decisions get made by committees in which everyone is voting tactically, assuming they know how others will vote, and the outcome is something no individual wanted. If your company makes significant decisions by group vote without anyone owning the recommendation, you are running the Swope mechanism and will eventually get a Swope result.

The second is what happens to his principles. He starts with a clear rule about which accounts he will not take, and the rule dissolves under commercial pressure, one justified exception at a time.

That is the normal failure mode for stated values, and the defence against it is not stronger conviction. It is writing the rule down specifically enough that an exception has to be argued openly, with somebody named as the person who approved it.

## 09 Songs

Songs that are about advertising, selling, media and wanting things. Not songs used in ads. Songs about the business of it.

### This Note's for You. Neil Young (1988)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/this-notes-for-you/
Date: 2026-09-06. Read: 3 min.

A refusal to sell songs to sponsors, with a title that parodies a beer slogan. MTV initially declined to air the video, then gave it Video of the Year in 1989. It is the clearest artefact of the moment when musicians had to decide whether sponsorship was selling out.

## What the song is about

Young attacks the practice of musicians licensing their work and their image to brands, naming the mechanism rather than any particular act. The title plays on a beer advertising line of the period, which is the joke and the accusation at once.

The video, directed by Julien Temple, parodied contemporary celebrity endorsement advertising closely enough that it ran into trouble before it ran anywhere.

## Why it belongs in a marketing reference

Because it marks the point where the terms of the argument changed.

In 1988 taking brand money was still a reputational question for a musician. Within a decade it was a revenue line, and within two it was the revenue line, as recorded music income collapsed and sync licensing and sponsorship replaced it. Young lost the argument comprehensively, and the song is the best record of what was being argued.

The MTV sequence is the part worth noticing. A channel funded entirely by advertising first refused to broadcast a song attacking advertising, then awarded it the top prize. Both decisions were commercially rational and they point in opposite directions, which is a fair description of how the industry has handled the question ever since.

## The honest complication
