Young's position was available to him because he was already wealthy and established. The artists for whom sponsorship money matters most are the ones with the least leverage to refuse it, and the song does not engage with that.

It is a principled position taken from a comfortable place, which does not make it wrong and does make it easier to hold.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The transferable question is about endorsement and what it costs the endorser.

When your company pays somebody to be associated with it, a creator, an industry figure, a customer in a case study, you are asking them to spend credibility they built elsewhere. That credibility is why the association is worth anything to you.

Which means two things follow. If you squeeze the arrangement so the person looks bought, the asset you were buying disappears in the act of buying it. And if the association later embarrasses them, you have taken something you cannot give back.

The practical version: pay properly, disclose clearly, and give the person genuine latitude to describe the work in their own words including the parts that were difficult. An endorsement that reads as controlled is worth very little, and everyone can tell.

### Sell Out. Reel Big Fish (1996)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/sell-out/
Date: 2026-09-02. Read: 3 min.

A ska-punk band signs to a major label and writes a hit about signing to a major label. The commercial bargain, sung cheerfully from inside it. It is the funniest entry in this section and the one that best describes how the argument actually ended.

## What the song is about

The decision to take the money, narrated without much agonising. The narrator leaves a day job, signs the deal, and reports that this is fine. The irony is that the song itself became the band's commercial breakthrough, which makes it either the perfect joke or the perfect demonstration, depending on how generous you feel.

## Why it belongs in a marketing reference

Because it is the other side of the Neil Young argument and it won.

Young's position was that taking brand money corrupts the work. This song's position is that the alternative to taking the money is not purity, it is a day job, and that the people most insistent about selling out are rarely the ones being offered anything.

Eight years separate the two songs and the shift in the register is complete. By 1996 the question was not whether to commercialise but how openly to admit it, and the admission itself became the marketable thing.

That move, turning the compromise into the product, is now a standard brand technique. Self-aware advertising that acknowledges it is advertising works for the same reason this song worked: it removes the audience's objection by stating it first.

## The honest complication

The joke relies on the band being genuinely uncertain whether they had sold out, and that uncertainty is not available to a company. When a brand performs self-awareness about being a brand, it is a tactic rather than a confession, and audiences read the difference quickly.

Most corporate attempts at this register fail for that reason. The move requires something actually at stake.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The useful idea here is pre-emption: naming the objection before your audience does.

In B2B this is close to free and almost nobody uses it. If your price is higher than the alternatives, say so and say why, in the first paragraph. If your product does not suit smaller companies, write that down. If a reference client had a difficult first quarter with you, put it in the case study.

Every one of those feels like handing the buyer a reason to say no. In practice it does the opposite, because the buyer already suspects it, and hearing it from you is the only evidence available that the rest of what you say is true.

The limit is the one the song illustrates. This works when the admission costs you something real. Performed candour, an admitted flaw that is secretly a boast, is worse than silence and everyone can smell it.

### Television, the Drug of the Nation. The Disposable Heroes of Hiphoprisy (1992)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/television-the-drug-of-the-nation/
Date: 2026-08-27. Read: 3 min.

Michael Franti's spoken-word indictment of broadcast media, consumption and attention, written before the feed replaced the channel. It is the most analytically serious song in this section and the one that has aged into something closer to prophecy than protest.

## What the song is about

An extended attack on television as a system: what it does to attention, what it does to political understanding, and whose interests it serves. The argument is structural rather than moral. Franti is not objecting to bad programmes, he is objecting to the medium's economics.

The central claim is that an advertising-funded medium cannot be a neutral information source, because its product is the audience rather than the programming.

## Why it belongs in a marketing reference

Because the argument it makes about television is now the standard critique of the attention economy, and it was made in 1992 about a medium that looks quaint.

Everything the song attacks, the optimisation for engagement over understanding, the conflict between an advertiser-funded model and the public interest, the measurement of people as audience inventory, transferred intact from broadcast to the feed and got substantially worse.

For anyone working in media buying it is a useful discomfort. The critique is not of advertising creative. It is of the business model that pays for all of our work, and it is not a stupid critique.

## The honest complication

The song treats the audience as passive, acted upon by the medium. The evidence on media effects is more complicated than that and has been for decades. People are harder to influence than either the critics or the industry tends to claim.

It is also a long argument delivered without much room for disagreement, which is the nature of the form and does mean it persuades by conviction rather than by evidence.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

There is a practical point buried in a thirty-year-old protest record.

If your company's growth depends on buying attention in advertising-funded environments, your cost base is tied to platforms whose incentives are not aligned with yours. They are optimising for time spent, not for whether your buyer understood anything. That is why attention gets more expensive every year while its quality does not improve.

The strategic response is not to stop buying media. It is to notice how much of your reach you rent and how much you own. An audience you reach through a platform can be repriced or removed without notice. An audience that has given you their email address, or that comes to something you publish, cannot.

Most B2B companies rent almost all of it and have never looked at the ratio. It is a single number and it is worth asking for.

### Money. Pink Floyd (1973)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/money/
Date: 2026-08-21. Read: 3 min.

Roger Waters on greed, written by a band about to become extremely rich from it. The irony was noted at the time, including by Waters, and the song is more interesting for that than for its argument.

## What the song is about

An unreliable narrator enumerating what money buys and what he intends to buy with it. The satire is obvious on the surface. What makes the song last is the production: it is built on a cash register loop in an unusual time signature, so the mechanism of transaction is literally the rhythm the song runs on.

That is a better piece of sound design about commerce than anything in advertising.

## Why it belongs in a marketing reference

Two reasons, and the second is the real one.

It is the most commercially successful song about money ever recorded, from an album that sat on the charts for a decade and a half, which is a joke the band have never been able to escape.

More usefully: it is a case study in how a critique becomes a commodity. "Money" is now licensed, soundtracked, played in bars, and used in exactly the contexts it was attacking. Nothing about the song changed. The culture simply absorbed the criticism and sold it, which is the thing Franti warned about and the thing Neil Young refused to participate in.

The lesson for anyone building a brand on a critical position: the critique is absorbable. Being against something is not a durable differentiator, because the thing you are against can usually just buy the aesthetic.

## The honest complication

Waters has been open about the contradiction and it does not really damage the song. Writing about greed while becoming rich is not hypocrisy, it is the only vantage point from which the subject is visible.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The commercial idea here is that positioning against something is weaker than it feels.

Challenger positioning is attractive, particularly for a smaller firm. We are not like the big incumbents, we are transparent where they are opaque, we are senior-led where they are leveraged. It reads well and it wins meetings.

The problem is that it is borrowed. Your position is defined by what the incumbent does, so when they change, or simply adopt the language, your position evaporates and you have no independent description of yourself. Large firms adopt challenger language constantly and at no cost, because it is only language.

The durable version is a position that describes what you are rather than what you are against, and that would still make sense if every competitor disappeared tomorrow. That is harder to write and it is the only kind worth having.

Test: remove every comparative from your positioning statement. If nothing survives, you have a critique rather than a position.

### Material Girl. Madonna (1984)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/material-girl/
Date: 2026-08-15. Read: 3 min.

A song about valuing men by their money, performed by an artist who then spent four decades demonstrating control over her own commercial image. The song is slight. What happened around it is the reason it belongs here.

## What the song is about

A narrator who states plainly that she is interested in wealth, delivered without apology. Written by Peter Brown and Robert Rans, not by Madonna, which is worth knowing because the public reading has always treated it as autobiography.

The video, directed by Mary Lambert, restages the Marilyn Monroe diamonds number from Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, and the framing device has the suitor win her with a cheap bunch of flowers rather than jewellery. The video contradicts the song. Almost nobody remembers the contradiction.

## Why it belongs in a marketing reference

Because it is the clearest demonstration available that the audience takes the hook and discards the qualification.

The song had an ironic frame. The video had a counter-argument built into its plot. Neither survived contact with the public, which extracted three words, attached them to the artist permanently, and ignored everything else. Madonna has spent forty years being described by a phrase from a song she did not write.

For anyone writing marketing copy this is the most useful cautionary tale in the section. If your message has a clever qualification, assume the qualification will be lost and only the blunt part will travel. That is not an argument against nuance. It is an argument for making sure the blunt part is something you are willing to be known by.

## The honest complication

The reading above is tidy and the reality is that the association was also commercially useful to her for a long time. Being misread as a material girl was not obviously a cost. Artists and brands can profit from a simplification they did not choose, and pretending otherwise is sentimental.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

The practical lesson is about what survives compression.

Every description of your company gets shortened as it travels. Your positioning statement becomes a sentence, the sentence becomes a phrase, and the phrase is what a prospect repeats to a colleague who was not in the room. You do not control the compression and you cannot add a footnote to it.

So the test for any positioning is not whether it is accurate in full. It is what survives when it is cut to five words by somebody who was half listening.

Try it. Ask three people who know your business to describe it in one short sentence, without preparation. The variation in their answers is your real positioning, and if it contains a flattering oversimplification you have not chosen, that is now part of your brand whether you like it or not.

This is also why qualifying language in marketing tends to be wasted effort. The qualifier is the first thing dropped.

### Advertising Space. Robbie Williams (2005)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/advertising-space/
Date: 2026-08-09. Read: 2 min.

A song about the afterlife of a famous person's image, and what happens to it once they are no longer there to object. The commercial subject is posthumous licensing, which is a real and growing industry and is almost never written about.

## What the song is about

Fame as a property that outlives the person, and the emptiness of the estate that remains. The reference point is Elvis Presley, and the title is the central image: a person reduced to space that can be sold.

## Why it belongs in a marketing reference

Because posthumous endorsement is an actual market and most marketers have never thought about it.

Dead celebrities are licensed routinely. Estates manage image rights, approve or decline associations, and generate substantial revenue from people who cannot consent to any of it. The legal position varies considerably by jurisdiction: some recognise a descendible right of publicity, others do not, and the differences create a patchwork that is mostly navigated by whoever has the better lawyers.

The ethical question is not complicated and is rarely asked. A living endorser chooses the association. A dead one cannot, and the person choosing on their behalf has a financial interest in saying yes.

Williams, writing as someone whose own image is a managed asset, is closer to the subject than most commentators.

## The honest complication

The song is sentimental about Presley in a way that obscures the argument. Presley's image was heavily commercialised while he was alive and with his participation, so the contrast between the authentic living person and the exploited estate is weaker than the song needs it to be.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

Narrow and practical: check what your contracts say about using people's images and words after they leave.

Most companies hold testimonials, case study quotes, headshots and video from employees and clients, obtained with informal consent, and keep using them indefinitely. The person leaves the client, changes career, retires, or dies, and the asset stays in the deck.

Three things worth confirming. Whether your consent forms are time-limited or perpetual. Whether they survive the person leaving the company they were at. And who in your business is responsible for removing material when consent is withdrawn, because in most firms nobody is and the request goes to whoever answers the email.

This is a small administrative matter until the day it is not, and the day it is not usually involves somebody's family.

### Don't Believe the Hype. Public Enemy (1988)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/dont-believe-the-hype/
Date: 2026-08-03. Read: 3 min.

Chuck D attacking the media's account of his own group, from an album that argued the press was not a neutral narrator but a participant with interests. It is the best song ever written about media relations, which is not a crowded field.

## What the song is about

A direct response to press coverage of Public Enemy, arguing that the reporting was hostile, inaccurate and shaping public understanding in ways the group could not correct through the same channels.

The title entered general English as a phrase, which is itself a demonstration of the group's argument about who gets to set the terms.

## Why it belongs in a marketing reference

Because it describes the structural problem of earned media from the side of the subject, and that perspective is almost entirely absent from marketing literature.

Public relations is usually taught as the management of relationships with journalists. This song describes what it feels like to be covered by people whose incentives differ from yours, whose account reaches more people than your own, and who are under no obligation to be right.

Chuck D's famous description of rap as a news medium for a community the mainstream press was not serving is the other half of the argument. If the existing channel misrepresents you, the response is to own one.

That is now standard advice. Build an audience you reach directly rather than depending on intermediaries. The song made the case forty years before it became a content marketing slide.

## The honest complication

The owned-channel answer solves the distribution problem and not the credibility problem. An account of yourself that you publish is discounted precisely because you published it, which is why third party coverage retains its value despite being harder to control.

Both things are true: you need a channel you own, and the thing that persuades is still somebody else saying it.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

There is a decision here that most companies never make deliberately.

How much of your reputation depends on intermediaries describing you accurately, and what is your alternative if they do not? Trade press, analysts, review sites, and now AI assistants all produce accounts of your company that reach more people than anything you publish, and none of them is obliged to be correct.

The owned channel is the standard answer and it is only half an answer. A newsletter, a research report, a reference site: these give you distribution you control. They do not give you credibility, because you wrote them.

The combination that works is owning the primary material and letting other people cite it. Publish the data, the method, the thing nobody else has, and let the intermediaries use it. Then the account that reaches people is written by somebody else and sourced from you, which is the only version that does both jobs.

That is a slower strategy than a campaign and it is the one that compounds.

### Radio Radio. Elvis Costello (1978)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/radio-radio/
Date: 2026-07-28. Read: 3 min.

An attack on commercial radio as a gatekeeper, from an artist who then performed it on live American television after being told not to. The performance is more famous than the song and both belong here.

## What the song is about

Radio as an institution that presents itself as serving an audience while actually serving advertisers and its own commercial interests. The complaint is about gatekeeping: a small number of programmers deciding what reaches everyone, with incentives that have nothing to do with quality.

## Why it belongs in a marketing reference

The Saturday Night Live incident in December 1977 is the part worth knowing. Costello began a different song, stopped it after a few bars, and led the band into this one instead, against the wishes of the programme. He was reportedly banned from the show for a long period afterwards.

That is a complete case study in channel risk in about ninety seconds. An artist dependent on a platform for reach, using the platform to attack gatekeeping, and losing access to it as a direct result.

Every company that builds its distribution on a platform it does not own is in the same position, with less drama and the same mechanics. The platform sets the terms, the terms change without negotiation, and the cost of objecting is removal.

## The honest complication

Costello could afford it. He had a recording contract and a touring base, so losing one television show was survivable. Most people and most companies dependent on a channel do not have that, which is exactly why they comply.

The song is a principled stand by somebody with an alternative. The useful question is what you would do without one.

## If you run the company rather than the marketing

This is the clearest statement in the section of a risk most companies carry and never price.

If a single channel delivers most of your pipeline, whether that is paid search, one platform's organic reach, a marketplace, a referral partner or now an AI assistant, you do not have a marketing strategy. You have a dependency, and the owner of that channel can change its terms at any point without consulting you.

The test is one number: what proportion of new business arrived through your single largest channel last year? If it is above half, that is the most significant commercial risk in the business and it probably does not appear on any risk register, because it only looks like a risk in the quarter it stops working.

The remedy is not to abandon the channel that works. It is to deliberately fund a second one before you need it, accepting that it will look inefficient by comparison for a long time. That comparison is the trap: the efficient channel is efficient right up until it is gone.
